title: The platform-admin login stamps a claim of its own, so the gateway can refuse tenantless tokens except platform admins (KS-619 follow-up)
description:
**BLUF:** KS-619 needs a marker that does not exist yet. The gateway should refuse a token that carries no tenant, except for a platform admin; but nothing in a platform admin's token says it came from the platform-admin login, and the roles that login mints are not in the shared platform-role list, so a refusal keyed on role locks them out of the whole gateway. The fix Kam chose: the platform-admin login stamps one claim that only that branch sets; the gateway's tenant refusal excepts it; refresh tokens carry it; platform admins re-login once after it deploys. Two services (auth and api-gateway), tier 1, security. Kam ruled the split on 2026-11-09 17:20:38 (card `secuura-ks619-platform-admin-login-no-marker-1109`, option a, "Split"); the tenant-refusal half of KS-619 comes out of PR 2128, which keeps only the user-id and role guard (no lockout), and this ticket carries the rest.

## The ruling, quoted

Kam, verbatim (live board, 17:20:38): "Decision secuura-ks619-platform-admin-login-no-marker-1109: a — Split". Option a: "PR 2128 keeps only the user-id and role guard (no lockout). KS-619 becomes its own ticket: the platform-admin login stamps one claim and the gateway excepts it. Two services, tier 1; platform admins re-login once after it deploys."

## Facts, each with its source

1. **The refusal locked a population out (gate 285, finding G285-1, MEDIUM).** Source: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-09_gate285-tier1-pr2128-ks1208-ks619/verdict.md`, from line 21, on PR 2128 head `aff0f43e4079`. The login issues the roles `platform_admin`, `platform_viewer` and (the Azure default) `admin`, with no tenant. The shared `isPlatformRole` (`Blockchain/Dev/packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts`) is false for all three (the gate measured it with node on the built dist; controls `super_admin`, `system_admin` and `Super_Admin` are true). With the refusal in place and a token shaped as that login mints it, the gate's cells read: platform_admin on a required mount, develop 200 and head 401; platform_viewer on a required and on an optional mount, develop 200 and head 401; controls (a super_admin with no tenant, and an owner token) unchanged. It fails closed, so the gate did not call it a hole.
2. **Reach was not measured.** The gate did no live count. The note in KS-1536 says a Kintsugi count found no `platform_admin` rows on that path; `platform_viewer` and `admin` were not counted, and Azure was never counted.
3. **The code today, re-read by me.** At develop `6beac8734a2f` (Wednesday's addendum cites Seat G 31st's read of the same lines), the platform-admin login in `Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/routes/auth.ts` builds its `syntheticUser` with `tenantId: undefined` and `tenantSlug: undefined` (lines 394 to 410) and mints with `role: platformAdmin.role` (lines 470 to 473). `generateAccessToken` in `Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/services/jwt.ts` (lines 187 to 209) builds one claim set for every login mint (`userId`, `email`, `role`, `organizationId`, `verificationLevel`, `sessionId`, `type`, `tenantId`, `tenantSlug`, then scopes or the OAuth labels), and `signToken` (lines 175 to 182) signs with the single provisioned key with no issuer or audience option. So no claim distinguishes a platform-admin login from any other mint, which is why the refusal had to go by role.
4. **The build shape is Kam's** (card above, option a): the login stamps one claim only that branch sets; the gateway's tenant refusal excepts it; refresh tokens carry it; platform admins re-login once after the deploy. Which claim name and value, and how the gateway verifies it, are for the build to propose.

## Not done, not measured

No live count of platform-admin rows (point 2). I did not re-read the gateway's present handling of a token with no tenant claim, or the refresh-token path. Nothing was run.

## Related

KS-619 (the gateway falls through to the caller's tenant header when a token has no tenant claim; this ticket is its remaining half) and KS-1208 (a verified token without a role or userId claim; PR 2128 delivers its guard). Both are linked as related.

## Searched before filing

Board, includeArchived, title and description and every comment of each open candidate; controls pass (the positive control hit its known ticket KS-1379, a random token hit 0). `KS-619`: 13 candidates, 10 open literal hits (KS-621, KS-1032, KS-1084, KS-1091, KS-1536, KS-1553, KS-1673, KS-1704, KS-2109, KS-2145), none a ticket for a login claim; KS-619 itself was read (its description to 2,600 characters and its two newest comments). `platform-admin login`: 94 candidates, 5 open (KS-783 and KS-919 on TOTP recovery and the demo account's MFA, KS-1132 on an infrastructure failure read as no admin, KS-1384, KS-2120): KS-2120 was read, it rewords one comment about this login (PR 2112) and carries no claim work. `tenantless token`: 93 candidates, 4 open (KS-1406, KS-1652, KS-1655, KS-1740): KS-1406 was read, it is the users lookup and stub guard that fails open for a tenantless token, a different route and fix. `platform_admin`: 108 candidates, 18 open, judged by title and search context; the near neighbours are KS-1536 (the role vocabulary) and KS-1132. No open ticket carries the claim-and-exception work.

title: api-gateway: admin-minted connector keys share the identity connector:api-key, so one tenant's key can list and delete another's inbox rows
description:
**BLUF:** Admin-minted API keys carry no connector id, so the gateway gives every one of them the same `userId`, `connector:api-key`. Gate 246 measured that tenant B's key can then list, and delete, a notification row that tenant A's key placed in that inbox. PR 2072 (KS-1448, merged as `7eda23b34d3b`) now refuses a `userId` other than the caller's, with a connector key allowed its own id; for this population "its own id" is the shared one, so that ruling does not close it. The identity sharing predates PR 2072, which narrows the route. High is Wednesday's call.

Source: gate 246 (PR 2072, KS-1448), finding 72-1, recorded by Wednesday as G246-F1: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-07_gate246-tier1-services/verdict.md`, and her note `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/2_Project_Files/fleet/briefs_staged/2026-11-08_B99_answer_notes_2072.md`. Every line number below I read myself at develop `7eda23b34d3b7a413ca8f9c0945c7843708ce9f4`, which is the merge of PR 2072.

1. Where the identity comes from. `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/middleware/auth.ts` line 572 builds `userId: connector:${meta.connectorId || 'api-key'}`, and line 312 sets `connectorId: data.connectorId || ''`. The comment at lines 52 to 55 of the same file says `connectorId` is null for admin-minted keys, so every such key gets the one userId `connector:api-key`: "one bucket across all tenants".
2. What PR 2072 ruled. `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/routes/notifications.ts` lines 315 to 327: `if (userId !== getUserId(req))` answers 403 for every principal, and a connector key may create for its own id. For a key with no connector id, its own id is `connector:api-key`, the same string for every such key of every tenant. Neither the PR nor its ticket comment says so.
3. The steps. Evidence class: MEASURED at runtime by gate 246, for the route through the real `authenticateToken` with the security service's answer stubbed to `connectorId: null`. (1) Key A, of tenant A, posted `type: security` with an `actionUrl` to `connector:api-key`: 201. (2) Key B, of tenant B, listed the row: 200. (3) Key B deleted it: 200. (4) Key A posting to `victim`: 403, so PR 2072's rule holds for every other id.
4. Not measured. Whether admin-minted keys exist on any live box, and whether anyone reads such an inbox. The gate notes that connector inboxes are unlikely to have human readers.

Shared root: every API key without a connector id is the one principal `connector:api-key`. KS-1685 records that for vc-issuer and says cross-tenant stays separated there; the notification routes act on that string with no tenant check, as measured above, so here it does not. The transfer service's `GET /api/notifications` has the same root: KS-2119.

Fix shapes, the gate's: refuse admin-minted keys on this route, or derive a per-key id; at minimum, name the gap, which this ticket does. The regression test to add: two keys with null `connectorId` cannot see each other's rows.

Not claimed: no run by me, and no reading of any live box.

Related: KS-1448 (PR 2072's ticket; the facts-only line to Peter about his strict xfail marker goes there separately, after approval), KS-1685 (the shared principal), KS-2119 (the transfer-notification read), KS-2001 (the same fallback on an integrations lookup).

Priority: High, Wednesday's call.

Duplicate search before filing (board account, includeArchived; open tickets read with all comments; output in `/Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-09_seatS-38th/evidence/search_q1245.out` and `search_q1_more.out` in the same folder): `connector:api-key` 6 open: KS-1685, KS-2001 and KS-2081 read whole (none records the notification inbox; KS-1685 says cross-tenant stays separated for vc-issuer); KS-772, KS-843 and KS-1579 by title. `routes/notifications.ts` 5 open: I read KS-1448 whole (6 comments; no mention of the shared identity or of a second tenant), and KS-2076, KS-1346 and KS-1410 by title. `x-user-id` 9 open, other subjects. I found no ticket for the cross-tenant inbox.

title: Connector-key rotate answers rotated true with no warning while an older organisation key with no connector id still validates
description:
**BLUF:** The connector-key rotate (register-connector with rotate on) answers `rotated: true`, a count of 1 and no warning while an older key of the same organisation, one that carries no connector id, still validates. It happens on the retry after a count of 0, and also on the first call when the organisation holds both kinds of key, so no 0 is needed. The cause is in security's retire, which matches only the connector id; the gateway cannot see the older key. Gate 257 measured it on real PostgreSQL. It is old behaviour that PR 2073 narrows (the 0 itself is now honest) and does not remove. Priority High is Wednesday's call; the gate graded the finding Medium. Wednesday's ruling on the fix direction, under Kam's card `secuura-ks-1152-rotate-says-rotated-when-old-key-lives-1106` = b ("Keep rotating, but answer 'rotated: false' and say why", ruled 2026-11-06 15:00:34 AEDT, read with `tools/decision_queue.sh show`): the fix extends that honest answer to these keys; it does NOT retire them.

Source: gate 257, tier 1, round 2 of 2, PR 2073 (KS-1152 R-880-1), finding F1 and the section "For Kam, at the top", `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-08_gate257-tier1-pr2073-r2/verdict.md`, lines 17 to 34 and 40 to 49. Wednesday's ADDENDUM to the board seat, 2026-11-08 11:39:30Z, orders this filing. Seat Y 8th had recorded the retry case first (its probe P2, in its entry in `5_Project_History/history.md`) and proposed a distinct code for Kam's and Stuart's monthly agenda.

1. What was measured. Evidence class: MEASURED by gate 257 on real PostgreSQL 15 (the gate's own cluster), through a real gateway route over real security, at PR 2073's head `2684a29d8f576ff74634f07ad6576af5bd00370b` and again on the develop merge.
   * G2a, the first call with a count of 0: 200, `rotated` false, `priorKeysRevoked` 0, `PRIOR_KEY_STILL_ACTIVE`. The older key and the new key both validate.
   * G2b, the retry: 200, `rotated` true, count 1, no warning. The older key is still valid; the key the 0 call returned is no longer valid.
   * G3, an organisation that holds both an older key with no connector id and a key with the connector id, first call: 200, `rotated` true, count 1, no warning. The older key is still valid; the connector key is retired.
2. Where. Evidence class: READ. `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/routes/platform.ts` at PR 2073's head, line 979: `rotated: rotate && existing.rows.length > 0 && priorKeysRetired && priorKeysRevoked >= 1`. `Blockchain/Dev/services/security/src/index.ts` at develop `abd044f63a9dd5673f1b9ff7a2b1e42e1c26de82` (the file is not changed by PR 2073), lines 239 and 246: both retire statements end `WHERE connector_id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2::uuid AND id <> $3 AND is_active = true`, so a key with no connector id is never matched.
3. Why it is old behaviour. By the gate's reading, develop answers `rotated: true` on the 0 itself, on the retry and on G3. PR 2073 makes the 0 honest and leaves the retry and G3 as they were.
4. The fix direction. Ruled by Wednesday (ADDENDUM 11:39:30Z): extend the honest answer, `rotated: false` with a reason, to these keys; do not retire them. The gate's two fix shapes were that security reports how many active keys of the organisation remain after the retire, or that the retire also takes the organisation's keys that have no connector id. The first fits the ruling; the second is what the ruling excludes. A regression test the owner should add (the gate): G3's shape, asserting that `rotated` is not true while the older key validates. If this behaviour stays for now, the gate asks for one sentence each in `Blockchain/Dev/docs/S-K-OWNERSHIP-CONTRACT.md` and in the spec: "`rotated: true` says nothing about an older key with no connector id; a retry after a 0 answers `rotated: true` with that key still active."
5. The cost the gate names in Wednesday's ruling A2. One code now carries two instructions, so a client that reads only the code retries after a 0 and lands in G2. The PR body calls that retry "futile, not harmful"; the gate disagrees, because the retry ends in a false all-clear. The gate leaves that trade-off to Kam.
6. Who reads `rotated`. By the gate: rotation is platform-admin only (its GUARDRAIL 1), so a K admin reads the reply; whether Platform S reads `rotated` is unknown; the only code reader is systemTest, which stops at `rotated: true`. The contract Stuart's team reads says a retry does not help but not that the retry answers `rotated: true`, and it does not mention G3.

Not claimed: how many keys with no connector id exist on any box (the gate did not measure it); whether Platform S reads `rotated`; any run by me. PR 2073 is not merged: the line numbers for `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/routes/platform.ts` are at its head and may shift when it merges.

Related: KS-1152 (PR 2073's ticket, another seat's; I do not comment there). KS-1966 is the failed-retire case that PR 2073's round 1 answers, and KS-577 is revoke-on-rotate; I read both by title only.

Priority: High, Wednesday's call in the ADDENDUM.

Duplicate search before filing (board account, includeArchived, open tickets read with all comments): `PRIOR_KEY_STILL_ACTIVE` 1 open literal hit (KS-1152, PR 2073's own ticket); `priorKeysRevoked` 8 open (KS-577, KS-772, KS-1152, KS-1533, KS-1868, KS-1904, KS-1966, KS-2074); `rotationWarning` 1 open (KS-1152); `rotated: true` 2 open (KS-1152, KS-1966); `S-K-OWNERSHIP-CONTRACT` 4 open (KS-577, KS-1174, KS-1807, KS-1859) and 5 closed. KS-1966 is the failed-retire case, a lock timeout on the retire (I read its description), so another subject; KS-1152 is PR 2073's ticket; the others I read by title only. No ticket carries this finding. Output: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-08_seatS-37th/evidence/search_gate257.out`.

title: anchoring: an empty or null 2xx reply from a configured chain client reads ABSENT, which can lead to a second fee-paying transaction
description:
**BLUF:** with a configured chain client, a 2xx reply with an empty body or a JSON `null` counts as the chain answering and reads ABSENT in the anchoring confirmation poller, and a body of `{}` reads confirmed with no block hash. A false ABSENT lets guard 3 schedule the ordinary retry, which is a second fee-paying Cardano transaction; its fee and its on-chain record cannot be undone. QA gate 248 found it while gating PR 2081 (KS-1171 8k). It is older than that PR, which cannot add the outcome (1,364 attempt sequences, 0 widened). Kam's card `secuura-anchoring-second-fee-on-empty-reply-1107` = a, "Merge PR 2081, and fix the empty reply before anchoring next deploys (recommended)", ruled 2026-11-08 at 20:31:42 +11:00; its detail: "Two tickets by a board seat, High for the empty reply and Medium to measure the mint on an image. A build seat fixes the empty reply next, tier 1 gate. Anchoring's deploy stays held for your word." This is the High ticket. The Medium half is carried on KS-562, whose gate 70 comment already records the open question, "whether the anchoring image's install layout reproduces the split in a built container". Evidence class: MEASURED AT RUNTIME for the client and the poller result, with the real client and poller; guard 3's retry from this input follows from an existing cell's path (cell C1) and was not driven end to end.

**Measured (gate 248):** the real blockfrost-js 6.1.1 on a loopback listener returns an empty string for an empty 200 and for a 204, `null` for a body of `null`, and `{}` for a body of `{}`. HTML on a 200 throws; a 404 and a 502 throw with their status. The real provider and the real poller on the production schedule, at develop and at the PR 2081 head, with the transaction lookup resolving each body: an empty string and `null` give `polled` 30 and `definitelyAbsent` true; `{}` gives `confirmed` true with no block hash.

**Why it matters (gate 248):** the code's own comment defines an answer as "the transaction or not found". An empty 200 is neither. It is the same second-fee harm that PR 2081 closes for the no-client case, on the configuration that really pays fees, where 8k itself has no route. PR 2081's sentence "An empty 200 is '', so it still counts as an answer, as it does today" is true, but nothing there says it reaches guard 3.

**Likelihood (gate 248):** low. It needs an upstream or a proxy answering 2xx with no body. Not seen in service; no box was read.

**Where:** `Blockchain/Dev/services/anchoring/src/cardano/confirmation.ts`, lines 94 to 103 at the PR 2081 head (gate 248's tree). On develop `a65ae7ed1d60` the same polling logic starts near line 81, where the `polled` counter is incremented. Gate 248's probes are in the evidence folder next to its verdict.

**Fix shape (gate 248, for the owner):** decide whether the poller counts only `null` and a real transaction as answers, and pin it. That touches the 2026-09-25 definition of "answered" (card `secuura-ks1171-when-is-an-anchor-absent` = c); Kam's ruling above sends it to a build seat under a tier 1 gate. Anchoring's deploy stays held for Kam's word.

**Not measured:** a real Blockfrost, a real node or a real unreachable chain; any box, image or gateway path; guard 3's retry end to end from this input; how often a provider sends an empty 2xx.

**Source:** gate 248 verdict, finding F1 and the chain-cost section, `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-07_gate248-tier1-pr2081-ks1171/verdict.md`. This seat re-read the verdict and the line locations and ran nothing else. Related: KS-1171 (the ticket PR 2081 belongs to), KS-562 (the thread-token mint question).

**Board search (2026-11-08, closed and archived tickets included, paginated; controls held: the control term msgpackr hits KS-1379, a random token hits 0):** "definitelyAbsent": 1 open hit, KS-1171 (the mixed-window rule; a scan of its description and six comments for an empty or null body found none). The anchoring confirmation path: open KS-485 and KS-1171, closed KS-489 and KS-1810 (the reconciler's 24 h give-up cannot tell an outage from an absent transaction; a different matter). "empty 200": KS-485, KS-772 and KS-1673 (unrelated). No duplicate.

title: originate publishEvent swallows every Redis failure in an empty catch: a failed user.erased publish is silent and the log says published
description:
**BLUF:** originate publishes `user.erased` through its own `publishEvent`, and the `catch` at lines 143 to 145 of `Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/events.ts` is empty. A Redis failure while publishing is therefore silent: the erasure returns success, `gdprService` logs `user.erased event published`, and no stream entry exists, so no downstream service ever erases the subject's copy. With `REDIS_URL` unset the same happens. The `warn` branch in `gdprService` that says the cascade may be incomplete cannot fire on a Redis failure, because `publishEvent` never throws. Found in Seat U 17th's walk of the erasure; no fix here.

**Measured (MEASURED AT RUNTIME), Seat U 17th, 2026-11-06:** the real compiled originate on PostgreSQL 15.19 and redis-server 8.10.3 at develop `b7d433fda83c` on Node v26.8.1; not a box, not Kintsugi, not demo. Evidence file `/Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-06_seatU-17th/evidence/walk/run_erasure.out`, lines 12 and 13, quoted:

* `E8 dead Redis {"result":{"label":"E8","success":true,"tables":["users","pii_subject_keys"],"ms":89},"warned":false,"newEntries":0,"status":"deleted","walletKept":true}`
* `E9 REDIS_URL unset {"result":{"label":"E9","success":true,"tables":["users","pii_subject_keys"],"ms":95},"saidPublished":true,"newEntries":0}`

Seat U 17th predicted a `warn` for E8 before running it (`predictions_erasure.txt` line 10 in the same folder) and the run showed none: success true after 89 ms, no warn line, 0 stream entries, and the log line `user.erased event published`. Its STATUS of 2026-11-06 about 11:55Z (item W1) records the same.

**Where (READ at the same sha):**

* `Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/events.ts`: `publishEvent` (line 118) returns at once when there is no client (`if (!redis) return;`, line 123); otherwise its `try` runs `xadd` and the `catch` at lines 143 to 145 holds only the comment `// Fire-and-forget — never let event publishing break the service`. `initEventBus` warns once at start-up when `REDIS_URL` is unset (line 62); no later erasure says anything.
* `Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/services/gdprService.ts`: lines 962 to 981 wrap `await publishEvent(EventTypes.USER_ERASED, ...)` in a `try`, log `user.erased event published — downstream services will cascade` after it (line 970) and log `Failed to publish user.erased event (cascade may be incomplete)` in the `catch` (line 980). That `catch` is unreachable for a Redis failure.
* What does not happen when the entry is missing, per the same run: auth deactivating the user (E3) and wallet-connector deleting the wallet's session rows (E4); per KS-1955, kyc's deletes. KS-1955 also says originate marks the data-subject request completed at step 12, before the publish at step 13.

**Not measured:** a Redis failure that appears only after the `xadd` is accepted, and the running Kintsugi or demo originate (neither was touched).

**Board search (2026-11-06, includeArchived, paginated):** 0 open and 0 closed literal hits for `originate/src/events.ts` and `event published`. `user.erased` has 7 open hits, none about the publisher: KS-239, KS-485, KS-772, KS-1868, KS-1931, KS-1955, KS-2060. KS-1955 (Backlog, High, 0 comments) is the handler half: a failed kyc or wallet-connector handler after the bus, and its text does not name `Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/events.ts` or `publishEvent`. KS-2004 is an empty catch in the demo user seed, a different file. `publishEvent` appears in KS-1651 (the `ownership_transferred` payload) and `initEventBus` in KS-1868 (unguarded thrown-value reads); neither covers this empty catch.

**Possible shapes (mine, not a decision):** have `publishEvent` return whether the entry was added, or log inside the catch with the event type and the error message, and make the `gdprService` info line depend on that result so the existing `warn` can fire.

title: governance POST /api/governance/proposals/:id/execute checks no role: any signed-in user of any tenant executes a queued proposal
description:
**BLUF:** `POST /api/governance/proposals/:id/execute` checks only that the caller is signed in. It checks no role, no proposer or committee membership and no tenant. Measured on a real compiled service: a user of one tenant with the OWNER role executed a queued proposal created by a user of another tenant and got 200 with `status` `executed`. Limit: today execution only logs each action and flags it executed (no contract call), by Seat U 17th's read, so the effect is the proposal's status moving to `executed`. Found in Seat U 17th's walk of the governance service; no fix here.

**Measured (MEASURED AT RUNTIME), Seat U 17th, 2026-11-06:** the real compiled governance service on PostgreSQL 15.19 at develop `b7d433fda83c` on Node v26.8.1; not a box, not Kintsugi, not demo. Evidence file `/Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-06_seatU-17th/evidence/walk/run_base.out`, line 14, quoted (T1 and T2 are the two tenants of the walk):

* `X8 execute a T2 queued proposal as T1 OWNER {"s":200,"t2Status":"executed"}`

A 200 also means the timelock check passed, because the service answers 409 before the proposal's execution time. Sibling routes in the same walk do check the caller: cancel by a non-committee user answered 403 `Only proposer or constitutional committee can cancel` (line 11), and process-expired by an OWNER answered 403 where a SUPER_ADMIN got 200 (line 13).

**Where (READ at the same sha):** `Blockchain/Dev/services/governance/src/routes/governance.ts` lines 300 to 315: the handler reads `userId`, answers 401 when it is absent, and calls `governanceService.executeProposal(req.params.id, userId)`. `Blockchain/Dev/services/governance/src/services/governanceService.ts` line 1103: `executeProposal(proposalId: string, _executorId: string)`. The executor id is named `_executorId` and appears nowhere else in the file; the body checks that the proposal exists, is `queued` and is past its timelock, then marks its actions executed and saves.

**Not measured:** a rule in front of the service. The walk's STATUS lists originate, auth, wallet-connector and governance as the compiled services, so whether the api-gateway narrows this path is not measured.

**Board search (2026-11-06, includeArchived, paginated):** 0 open and 0 closed literal hits for `proposals/:id/execute`, `executeProposal` and `_executorId`. The nearest tickets are the same class on other services: KS-1814 (the document anchor route) and KS-2038 (the transfer doors).

**Possible shape (mine, not a decision):** a check like the cancel route's (proposer or committee) or a role set on `execute`, with a cell for the 403.

title: governance castVote counts a delegator's stake twice: the delegator still votes with it and the delegate's vote adds it again
description:
**BLUF:** In the governance service a delegator keeps full voting power after delegating it, and the delegate's vote adds the delegated power on top, so the same stake is counted twice in `votes_for`. Measured on a real compiled service: with one stake of 1000 delegated, `votes_for` reads 3000; in both controls (no delegation, and after the delegation is revoked) it reads 2000. Found in Seat U 17th's walk of the governance service; no fix here.

**Measured (MEASURED AT RUNTIME), Seat U 17th, 2026-11-06:** the real compiled governance service on PostgreSQL 15.19 at develop `b7d433fda83c` on Node v26.8.1; not a box, not Kintsugi, not demo. Evidence file `/Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-06_seatU-17th/evidence/walk/run_base.out`, lines 2 to 5, quoted (a is the delegator, d the delegate, each owns a stake of 1000):

* `4B control no delegation {"a":1000,"d":1000,"status":[200,200],"votesFor":2000}`
* `4B delegate {"s":200,"delegatedPower":1000}`
* `4B delegated {"a":1000,"d":2000,"status":[200,200],"votesFor":3000}`
* `4B after revoke {"a":1000,"d":1000,"votesFor":2000}`

The delegator's own vote was accepted (status 200) and counted 1000; the delegate's vote counted 2000, its own 1000 plus the delegated 1000.

**Where (READ at the same sha):** `Blockchain/Dev/services/governance/src/services/governanceService.ts`. `castVote` (line 946) gives every voter `voter.votePower` plus `getDelegatedPowerFor(voterId, proposal.category)` (lines 982 and 983) and nowhere checks whether the voter has delegated their own power away. `delegateVote` (line 1193) stores `delegatedPower: delegator.votePower` (line 1224) and leaves the delegator's own `votePower` as it was. `getDelegatedPowerFor` (line 1259) sums `delegatedPower` over the delegate's active delegations. The early-finalise check (lines 1038 to 1045 of the same file) reads `votesFor`, so the doubled figure can decide an outcome.

**Not measured:** a category-scoped delegation (`categories`), several delegators to one delegate, and a proposal whose outcome flips because of the extra power.

**Board search (2026-11-06, includeArchived, paginated):** 0 open and 0 closed literal hits for `getDelegatedPowerFor`, `delegated power` and `votes_for`. `castVote` has 0 open hits and 5 closed ones, none about delegation (KS-450, KS-1940, KS-1942, KS-1950, KS-1951).

**Possible shapes (mine, not a decision):** refuse or zero a delegator's own vote while an active delegation covers the proposal's category, or subtract the delegated-away power in `castVote`; either needs a test cell holding the 2000 and 3000 figures above.

title: OpenAPI examples after PR 782: five checks KS-256 left unchecked, and a LoginRequest example that locks its own account

title: Nothing schedules the base-image watch that the KS-365 ruling relies on: the cron is retired and the replacement script is run by hand
description:
**BLUF:** Kam's card on KS-365 accepts a critical vulnerability (CVE-2025-68121, in the gosu binary of the postgres:15-alpine image) on the strength of "the weekly image watch tells us when it clears". At source nothing runs a weekly watch: the workflow that ran it monthly is retired, and its replacement script is run by hand. Evidence class: READ ONLY. No fix shape is chosen here.

## Evidence

* **The card.** secuura-ks-365-postgres-image-gosu-vulnerability-1106, option a, "Accept until the upstream rebuild; re-scan weekly"; detail, verbatim: "No work; the weekly image watch tells us when it clears." Ruled 2026-11-06T14:59:40+11:00.
* **The workflow.** At develop 038e8ab5ae2d, read in a read-only clone: `.github/workflows/base-image-refresh.yml` opens "THIS WORKFLOW NO LONGER RUNS" and keeps only a workflow_dispatch trigger, with no cron. Its last scheduled run was 2026-08-01 (KS-365 comments db01e8bc and d27de4b7). GitHub Actions is retired for this repository (Kam, 2026-08-27).
* **The replacement.** `Blockchain/Dev/scripts/base-image-watch.sh` is run by hand. Its usage line calls the plain run "the monthly run", and KS-365 comment 8fe9efd6 says Wednesday runs it on the 1st of each month from a Secuura session. That is monthly and by hand, not weekly.
* **The last recorded re-scan.** KS-365 comment f00e3aa5 (2026-09-08): digest sha256:fe0737ba... unchanged, the CVE present. KS-365 records no re-scan after that date.
* **Board search**, includeArchived, by symbol (controls fired: the term msgpackr hits KS-1379; a random token hits 0). `base-image-watch`: 3 open literal hits and 3 closed. `base-image-refresh`: 2 open and 1 closed. The open hits are KS-365; KS-1446 (Renovate and EXCLUDED_BASES); KS-1669 (Renovate against the Dependabot ruling); and KS-636 (the node:24-alpine critical that the 2026-08-01 run flagged and nobody read). None of them owns scheduling the watch. KS-636 is the nearest, and was written on 2026-08-14, before Actions was retired.
* **Wednesday's scheduled jobs** were not found to run it, by Wednesday's read of her launchd list and scheduler folder just before her mail of 2026-11-06T05:45:38Z. Her read was a name grep, so it says little about a job under another name.

## UNMEASURED

* Whether anything outside the repository schedules the watch under another name. The instrument that closes it is the list of scheduled jobs read by what each job runs, not by its name.
* Whether the script has run at all since 2026-09-08. KS-365 records no run.
* Whether the hand run that KS-365 comment 8fe9efd6 describes happened on 2026-10-01 or 2026-11-01.

## Related

KS-365 (the ticket whose accepted residual relies on this watch) and KS-636 (the unread-alarm channel for the same watch). Who runs the watch, how often, and where a failure should land are not decided here.

title: Security: a demoted or deleted ORG_ADMIN or ISSUER_ADMIN whose token is still live can mint and revoke API keys (tenant-level and own organisation)
description:
## BLUF

A user whose token says ORG_ADMIN or ISSUER_ADMIN, and whose `users` row no longer holds that role or is no longer active, can still mint and revoke API keys: 201 and 200 on every shape measured, tenant-level and own-organisation alike. The key routes read no `users` row for these two roles. It is the same harm as KS-2032, for the two roles a login actually issues. KS-2032's predicate is ADMIN-only and its card rules ADMIN, so it does not reach them. Facts only; nothing is built. Whether the rule extends is Kam's.

## Measured

Seat Y 6th, 2026-11-06. The real `POST /api/keys` and `DELETE /api/keys/:id` on real PostgreSQL 15.19 as the least-privilege app role, on develop `299b9d6a3827` plus the KS-2032 working tree (which does not touch these two roles). Node v26.8.1, not an LTS line. Tokens hand-signed RS256: token role, tenant T, organisation A1, the user's id. Each row is one run of all four calls.

| token role | stored role / status | mint, no organisation | revoke a tenant-level key | mint for own organisation | revoke own organisation's key |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| ORG_ADMIN | org_admin / active (control) | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ORG_ADMIN | user / active | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ORG_ADMIN | verifier / active | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ORG_ADMIN | org_admin / deleted | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ORG_ADMIN | org_admin / suspended | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ISSUER_ADMIN | issuer_admin / active (control) | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ISSUER_ADMIN | user / active | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ISSUER_ADMIN | verifier / active | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ISSUER_ADMIN | issuer_admin / deleted | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |
| ISSUER_ADMIN | issuer_admin / suspended | 201, key created | 200, key inactive | 201 | 200 |

Instrument control: the same mint with a token for another tenant answers 403.

Evidence: `5_Project_History/2026-11-06_seatY-6th/evidence/ks2032/finding2_head.json`; the probe is `tools/ks2032_finding2_probe.integration.test.ts` in that folder. Evidence only, not committed to the repo.

## Read at source, not run

Lines at develop `299b9d6a3827`.

* `packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts:235`: for an org-bounded role, an unqualified target is allowed same-tenant. Kam's 2026-09-03 ruling for org-less keys.
* `services/auth/src/routes/users.ts:838`: an admin's change to a user revokes that user's sessions only when the new status forbids a credential. So a role-only demotion leaves the session alive.
* `services/api-gateway/src/middleware/auth.ts:672`: the gateway checks the session, not the `users` row, and fails open if the session store is unreachable. So through the gateway, a status shape above should die at 401 while the store is up, and a role-only demotion should not. Not run through the gateway.
* `services/auth/src/repositories/userRepo.ts:257`: `mapDbRole` issues ORG_ADMIN and ISSUER_ADMIN from stored rows, and has no key for ADMIN. So, by reading, these two roles are the ones real logins carry, and ADMIN is not (KS-2032's PR records that).
* `services/security/src/adminScope.ts:45`: `LIVE_ADMIN_USER_PREDICATE` is ADMIN-only and cannot serve these roles.

## Not measured

* A real demotion through `PATCH /api/users/admin/:id`, or any of this through the gateway.
* The real token lifetime on any box (compose default 1 day, code default 1 hour; the box values are not read).
* Whether any user on a box is in one of these states with a live token.
* Whether a tenant-level key reaches more than an organisation key: KS-2032's open item, still open.

## Open question (a decision, not made here)

Should these two roles also need a live `users` row holding that role at mint and revoke? It would be a new authorisation rule, not KS-2032's predicate, and it costs a database read on these roles' mints and revokes. Wednesday cards it for Kam with this figure.

Filed by Seat Y 6th on Wednesday's ANSWER 2026-11-06T05:02:31Z, from Finding 2 of the KS-2032 design QUESTION. Proposed priority: High. Related: KS-2032, KS-1585, KS-1570.

title: governance: an admin in one tenant can set stake and flags on another tenant's existing participant row
description:
**BLUF:** A platform admin in tenant T1 can change the stake, DRep status and committee status of a participant row owned by a user in tenant T2. QA gate 219 measured this at PR 2039 and at the develop before it, so it is not a regression. Nothing is fixed here. It needs a ruling, then a migration.

**Measured by the gate** (real compiled service, real JWT verification and router, real PostgreSQL as secuura_app):

* An admin in T1 on a row owned by a T2 user: 201, and stake, DRep and committee all change.
* One wallet linked in both tenants: the T1 admin binds it to the T1 user, the T2 owner gets 409, and a T2 admin's registration then writes onto the T1 user's row.

**Cause:** svc_governance_participants has no tenant column and no row-level security. Ruling D2 (a) on KS 1951 protects only the first bind, when no row holds the wallet yet. Once a row holds it, the admin path writes without reading a tenant. The comment in db.ts saying an admin in one tenant never binds another tenant's user is true only for a new row.

**What the ruling has to weigh:**

* **Precedent:** Kam's KS 1906 ruling keeps vc-issuer's owner-less credentials with "platform administrators of their tenant". Whether that reaches governance is not ruled.
* **The seeded SYSTEM_ADMIN sits in the default tenant** (userRepo.ts:1420). Today the only way that admin can stake a user in a provisioned tenant is this path: the owner self-registers, then the admin's stake lands on the row. Closing it plainly takes that away, so someone needs a named way to stake those users.
* **Other writers:** this was measured on the register route only. The other governance routes that read this table were not walked for the same shape.

**Fix shape, read only, not tried:** a tenant column on svc_governance_participants, backfilled from users, with row-level security and the same GUC the users read uses. A row whose id is not a user id (a legacy uuid row) has no tenant to backfill from, so it needs its own rule.

**Proposed priority:** High, because it writes vote power across a tenant boundary. The priority is for the humans to set.

title: transfer POST /api/delegations: parentDelegationId comes straight from the body and nothing ties it to the caller
description:
**BLUF:** `POST /api/delegations` takes the delegator from the authenticated user but passes `req.body.parentDelegationId` straight through, and the service checks only that the parent allows sub-delegation, has depth left and holds the permissions asked for; nothing compares the caller with the parent's delegatee, so any signed-in caller who knows a parent delegation id can create a child delegation under it. High. Priority as ruled by Wednesday (ANSWER 2026-11-06T03:40:16Z). Evidence class: READ ONLY at origin develop; the route was not run.

**Where**, at origin develop `45d2edc73aa9` (read 2026-11-06 by Seat S 27th with git show and git grep in a shallow scratch clone of origin develop `45d2edc73aa9`; nothing was run):

* `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/routes/delegations.ts` lines 60 to 80: `delegatorId` is read from `req.user` (line 64, 401 if absent); `createDelegationSchema.parse(req.body)` runs at line 69; the call at lines 71 to 75 passes `delegatorId`, the parsed body and `req.body.parentDelegationId` (line 74) to `createDelegation`.
* `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/services/delegationService.ts`: `createDelegation(delegatorId, request, parentDelegationId?)` from about line 187. The parent branch (lines 200 to 215) loads the parent, requires `canSubDelegate`, requires `currentDepth < maxDelegationDepth`, and requires the requested types to be a subset of the parent's. No line compares `delegatorId` with the parent's delegatee.
* I found no document-owner check in the route (lines 60 to 80) or in `createDelegation` up to line 220; I did not read past line 220.

**For the owner to decide:** require the caller to be the parent delegation's delegatee, and require ownership of the document for a top-level delegation.

**NOT measured:** the route at runtime; a real database; a gateway path; the service after line 220.

**Source:** Seat W 29th's QUESTION mail to Wednesday of 2026-11-06T02:47:04Z (section 5, item iii), re-read by Seat S 27th at the lines above.

**Board search before filing (2026-11-06, Seat S 27th, board_search tool, both controls held: 'msgpackr' hit KS-1379 among open tickets, a random token hit 0):** `parentDelegationId` returned 0 candidates; `createDelegation` 0 candidates. KS-1703 names a delegation read in its GET-by-id list; it does not cover creation.

title: transfer POST /api/transfers: the initiator names both parties in the body and nothing checks the caller is the current owner
description:
**BLUF:** `POST /api/transfers` (and `/api/transfers/initiate`) takes `currentOwnerId` and `newOwnerId` from the request body, validates only that each is a GUID, and copies both into the new transfer, so an authenticated caller can open a transfer that names someone else as the owner and themselves as the recipient. High. Priority as ruled by Wednesday (ANSWER 2026-11-06T03:40:16Z). Evidence class: READ ONLY at origin develop; the handler was not run.

**Where**, at origin develop `45d2edc73aa9` (read 2026-11-06 by Seat S 27th with git show and git grep in a shallow scratch clone of origin develop `45d2edc73aa9`; nothing was run):

* `Blockchain/Dev/services/transfer/src/index.ts` lines 375 and 376: `currentOwnerId: z.string().guid()` and `newOwnerId: z.string().guid()`. Line 528: `const initiatedBy = ((req as any).user?.userId as string) || data.currentOwnerId;` so the authenticated user feeds only `initiatedBy`, and the body's owner is the fallback. Lines 542 and 543 copy `data.currentOwnerId` and `data.newOwnerId` into the transfer. Lines 602 and 603 mount the handler on both paths. Nothing in the handler compares `currentOwnerId` with the caller or checks who owns `documentId`.
* Lines 580 to 582 create notifications for both named parties, so the named owner receives an approval-required notice for a transfer they did not start.

**Why it matters for KS-2038:** KS-2038 (the transfer routes approve, reject, execute and cancel admit any signed-in caller and take the actor from the body) depends on this ticket: any rule it adopts about who may act on a transfer reads `currentOwnerId` from the stored transfer, and this route lets the initiator set that value freely. The rule itself is not decided here and nothing in this ticket states it; the decision card for it is still open.

**Seat W 29th's reading (relayed in Wednesday's brief; not re-run by Seat S 27th):** binding `currentOwnerId` to the caller turns an existing object-authorization cell red, because that cell creates a transfer with an owner id that is not the caller.

**For the owner to decide:** bind `currentOwnerId` to the authenticated caller (or check ownership of `documentId`) at initiate, and refuse otherwise.

**NOT measured:** the handler at runtime; a real database; a gateway path; whether another service already checks document ownership before the gateway forwards this call.

**Source:** Seat W 29th's QUESTION mail to Wednesday of 2026-11-06T02:47:04Z (section 5, item i), re-read by Seat S 27th at the lines above.

**Board search before filing (2026-11-06, Seat S 27th, board_search tool, both controls held: 'msgpackr' hit KS-1379 among open tickets, a random token hit 0):** `initiateTransferHandler` returned 0 candidates. `currentOwnerId` and `newOwnerId` each returned one open literal hit, KS-1703, which names the two fields as part of the row a GET-by-id route returns; its scope is GET-by-id routes, not the initiate handler. Closed hits KS-466, KS-474 and KS-475 are earlier, different defects.

title: Pre-push cost: leg 14's 116 shell suites run one after another and are 90 to 92 percent of every push, and no other leg is timed
description:
BLUF: Every push that changes Blockchain/Dev runs all 16 preflight legs inside the push lock. Leg 14, the 116 shell suites, is 90 to 92 percent of it (948 of 1033 s, 990 of 1096 s, 1102 of 1213 s on three pushes read on 2026-11-06), they run strictly one after another, and no other leg is timed, so the other 85 to 111 s of each push is unattributed. At 03:26Z the push queue held 19 live tickets; at about 19 minutes a push that is several hours before the last of them reaches a gate.

One test pass, three items:

1. Per-leg timing. Blockchain/Dev/scripts/preflight/preflight.sh prints one line per leg for all 16 legs at the verdict, in leg order, each marked ran or skipped, with its seconds and a line stating the ratio of legs timed (16/16). The existing PREFLIGHT PASSED and PREFLIGHT FAILED lines, the legs ran count, the exit codes, the skip accounting and the shell suites wall-clock line stay byte-for-byte what they are. A failed run still prints the table.
2. Parallel suites, conditional on a measurement. First measure on this host whether the 116 suites collide when run side by side (fixed ports, shared postgres sockets, fixed names under /tmp) and what the saving is at several worker caps. Only if a safe set exists, Blockchain/Dev/scripts/run-shell-suites.sh runs it in parallel under a worker cap with buffered output printed in suite order. Every suite still runs. The pass, fail and skip rule, the empty-run refusal, the git environment clearing, the short TMPDIR substitution and --list and --check-unreached stay as they are; a worker cap of 1 reproduces today's serial output. New assertion: passed plus failed plus skipped must equal the suites reached. INT and TERM stop every running worker. bash 3.2 only. If the saving is small beside the added risk, item 2 is not raised and the numbers go on this ticket.
3. The push rehearsal runs leg 1 under the driver's own TMPDIR, so a hook-only failure like Seat V 24th's (a 121-byte tsx socket path against macOS's 104, lock held 18.6 minutes) shows in a rehearsal. This is a corrected tool copy in the seat's record folder, not part of the PR.

Not in scope: running the preflight outside the lock or pushing with --no-verify (Kam's card secuura-push-queue-prerun-preflight-1106, option a, is open; this work is its default, option b). This work reaches only branches cut after it merges, because the hook and the runner run from each pushing worktree's own tracked copy.

Source: Wednesday's push-queue cost report, 0_Brain/reference/2026-11-06_push-queue-cost/report.md (section 1 table and the UNMEASURED list).

Board search before filing (title and description, archived included, Secuura-PK): shell suites wall-clock 0 hits; per-leg timing 0; step() timing 0; worker cap 0; TMPDIR with rehears 0. Positive controls: run-shell-suites 28 hits, push queue 2 hits. Negative control, a nonsense symbol, 0 hits.

title: anchoring answers 202 during a database outage and the anchor has no row after recovery
description:
**BLUF:** In a Postgres outage on a disposable stack, anchoring answered 202 to 9 of 25 `POST /api/anchors` requests, and after recovery `anchor_store` held no row created after the stop. A 202 tells the caller its anchor was accepted. Split out of KS-2045 on Wednesday's ruling, because a crash loop and a 202 with no stored row are separate fixes. Nothing here is fixed.

## Measured

Seat U 16th, 2026-11-06, on throw-away stack `u16` built from develop `2fd6d529573c`, `NODE_ENV=development`, mock anchoring with no wallet. Not on a box. Postgres stopped 03:07:23Z for about 100 s, pgbouncer left running. A prober on the stack's internal network sent one `POST /api/anchors` every 4 s directly to anchoring, with a connector JWT minted on that stack.

* **9 of 25 answered 202.** The other 16 got connection, DNS or socket errors while the process was restarting (KS-2045).
* `anchor_store` **read at 03:11:30Z, about 2 minutes after Postgres was healthy: 0 rows created after the stop.** The newest row is 03:07:22.643Z. The 2 rows created just before the stop are there as the control, and the table holds 15 in all.
* **Anchoring's log in the outage:** `Database unavailable — using in-memory fallback` 9 times, `Anchor created` 9 times (2 more before the stop). The counts match the 9 responses; the prober kept statuses and not ids, so they were not matched one to one.
* **Each of those 9** `Anchor created` **lines is followed by the process crash in KS-2045 within 1 to 4 ms** (03:07:27.904Z to 03:08:42.469Z), so in this run no process that wrote one lived on. The row read is after the last restart.

## Read at source, not run

`Blockchain/Dev/services/anchoring/src/index.ts` at `2fd6d529573c`, in `dbPersistAnchor`:

* lines 1551 to 1552, a comment: "a failed persist must propagate so the handler returns a 5xx rather than a false 202".
* line 1553: `if (!isDbAvailable()) return { id: anchor.id, payloadTimestamp: payloadTimestampOf(anchor.metadataPayload) };`, which returns with no write.
* line 538: the handler calls it and carries on.

## UNMEASURED

* Whether anything later replays those anchors. The read came about 3 minutes after the last 202, and the stack was torn down at 03:13Z. That is why this ticket says "no row after recovery" and not "lost".
* How long an in-memory copy lives in a process that does not crash. Here each process crashed within 4 ms, so KS-2045 may be hiding what this path does on its own.
* Whether anything reaches a chain. This stack has no wallet, so nothing could from here; on a box, not measured.
* Kintsugi and demo, and `NODE_ENV=production`.
* The 202 bodies, and what a caller does on one. The prober kept statuses only.

## Searched before filing, 2026-11-06

Board search over titles, descriptions and comments, archived included:

* `using in-memory fallback`: open KS-1969 (auth sessions on Redis) and KS-2045 (where this was first written); closed KS-377.

title: Postgres outage behind pgbouncer kills auth, anchoring, api-gateway and tenant-provisioning on an unhandled pg client error
description:
**BLUF:** On a disposable stack, stopping Postgres with pgbouncer still up crash-looped auth and anchoring and restarted api-gateway and tenant-provisioning once each, on an unhandled pg client error. Callers saw 504 then 502, not the designed 503. With pgbouncer stopped too, auth stayed up and answered 503. Anchoring answered 202 nine times during the outage and those anchors have no row after recovery. Nothing here is fixed.

Found by Seat U 16th, 2026-11-06, running KS-1477's owed check, on throw-away stack `u16` built from develop `2fd6d529573c`, `NODE_ENV=development`, compose's own pgbouncer and Postgres, mock anchoring. Not on a box.

## Measured: run 1, requests through nginx and the gateway to auth

Postgres stopped 02:53:43Z, started 02:56:09Z, pgbouncer left running.

* auth: 9 restarts in about 2 minutes, crashing 1 to 2 s after each boot until Postgres came back; 18 `Unhandled 'error' event` lines in its log.
* api-gateway: `Uncaught exception` with `Connection terminated unexpectedly`, then shutdown and restart, once, at 02:55:28Z.
* What callers saw for `POST /api/users/me/verification`: 504 `GATEWAY_TIMEOUT` after 60 s, then 502 `BAD_GATEWAY`. Never the 503.

## Measured: run 2, requests in flight directly to four services

Postgres stopped 03:07:23Z for about 100 s, pgbouncer left running. A short-lived prober on the stack's internal network sent one request to each service every 4 s, bypassing the gateway. The baseline with the database up answered 201, 202, 200 and 200.

| service | restarts | in its log | what the prober saw (25 requests) |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| anchoring | **10** | `Unhandled 'error' event` 10, `Connection terminated unexpectedly` 10 | 202 on 9; connection, DNS or socket errors on 16 |
| tenant-provisioning | **1** | `Unhandled 'error' event` 1, `terminating connection due to administrator command` | 500 on 23; connection refused on 2 |
| originate | 0 | none of these | 500 on 25, `Code: 08P01`, `server login has been failing` |
| security | 0 | none of these | 503 on 25 |

* auth and api-gateway had nothing in flight to them in run 2 and did not restart.
* **Anchoring's 202s:** read at 03:10Z, after recovery, `anchor_store` holds 0 rows created after the stop; its newest row is 03:07:22Z, from the baseline, and the 2 baseline rows are there as the control. Its log says `Database unavailable — using in-memory fallback` 9 times. So 9 anchors were accepted with 202 and have no row. Whether that is this defect or its own is not decided here.
* Every service read healthy again within about a minute of Postgres returning.

## Discriminating control

With pgbouncer **and** Postgres stopped, so no established connection can be cut: auth logged 0 crashes and stayed up, including when restarted during the outage (the in-memory fallback line once), and answered 503 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` every time. Only auth was driven in this arm.

## The stack, verbatim, from auth

```
throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event
Error: Connection terminated unexpectedly
    at Connection.<anonymous> (/app/node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:204:73)
Emitted 'error' event on Client instance at:
    at Client._handleErrorEvent (/app/node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:422:10)
```

It holds no application frames.

## A reading, not measured

* It reads as a pg client checked out of a pool when pgbouncer cuts its connection ("server login has been failing"). The pool-level `on('error')` handlers would not cover a checked-out client.
* auth and the gateway died with a request in flight to them in run 1 and did not in run 2. That suggests in-flight work is the trigger; two runs do not establish it.

## UNMEASURED

* The call site in each service.
* Kintsugi and demo. Compose has the same pgbouncer; nothing was tried on a box.
* `NODE_ENV=production`.
* Every service not on this stack. Run 2 clears nothing: originate and security did not die under one request every 4 s, and a heavier or longer load was not tried.

## Searched before filing, 2026-11-06

Board search over titles, descriptions and comments, archived included:

* `Connection terminated unexpectedly`: open KS-1587 and KS-1960, closed KS-1188, none about this.
* `Unhandled 'error' event`: closed KS-1185 only.
* `pool.on('error')`, `client.on('error')`, `server login has been failing`, `terminating connection due to administrator command`: 0 hits each.
* `crash-loop`: open KS-485, KS-1079, KS-1982, none about a database outage.

Controls on the same instrument: `mobile/secuura-app` hit KS-1981 and a random token hit 0.

Evidence: `5_Project_History/2026-11-06_seatU-16th/evidence/ks1477/` and `evidence/crash_remeasure/`.

title: api-gateway: after a Redis eviction GET /api/admin/settings and GET /api/verification/policy read only Redis and serve the defaults, so a settings round trip can replace the stored allow-lists
description:
**BLUF:** In api-gateway at develop `07a2d62be6a0`, `GET /api/admin/settings` reads the `platform-settings` key from Redis directly, not through the settings store. After an eviction it serves the four default categories with no `integrations` key, although the stored record still holds the configured settings. `PUT /api/admin/settings` does read the stored record on a miss and merges `{ ...defaults, ...existing, ...body }`, so a body key replaces the stored key whole. A client that saves what the GET showed, with `integrations: []`, replaces the stored allow-lists with an empty list. `GET /api/verification/policy` makes the same direct Redis read. This is Seat E 35th's candidate 1 for PR 2001 (its "item 7").

Source: /Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-11-04_gate189-ks1256-pr2001/ready_2001.txt, CANDIDATES FOR FILING, item 1.

## Where (read at develop `07a2d62be6a0`, `Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/routes/admin.ts`)

* Lines 1150 to 1159: `redisService.getNotificationSettings('platform-settings') || {}`, laid over `PLATFORM_SETTINGS_DEFAULTS`.
* Lines 1184 to 1197: the PUT reads through `readPlatformSettings` (stored record on a miss) and merges with `...body` last.
* Lines 1216 to 1228: `GET /api/verification/policy` reads Redis directly and answers the built-in defaults on a miss or a throw.
* The defaults object (`Blockchain/Dev/services/api-gateway/src/services/settingsStore.ts` lines 38 to 43) holds `general`, `security`, `notifications` and `blockchain`; no `integrations`.

## Measured

Not by gate 189: its findings G189-F1 to F7 do not include this. The READY mail lists it as a candidate. This seat read the code only.

KS-1256 already names the two direct readers: its comment `de80f9b8` (2026-10-06) lists them as "the other readers", and its comment `6d4b1366` (2026-11-04, Seat W 24th, read at `ee1e1b832115`, "read, not measured") restates them by function: `GET /api/admin/settings` "a missing key serves the defaults as if they were stored", and `GET /api/verification/policy` "a missing key, or a throw, answers the defaults", with the line "Left open: ... The other readers are listed above." That text predates PR 2001. What this ticket records is the state at `07a2d62be6a0`: both direct readers are unchanged, and PR 2001 changed `PUT /api/admin/settings` to read the stored record on a miss, which is what makes a round trip of the GET's content replace the stored allow-lists.

## Grade

Low, this seat's judgement. It needs an admin client that round-trips the whole document, and whether one exists is not measured.

## Not measured

* Any run of the GET after an eviction, or of the round trip.
* Whether any admin UI or script sends the whole document back, or sends `integrations`.
* Whether a configured `verification` category is stored in any environment.
* This seat ran no test and no service; the code facts are reads of a depth-1 clone at `07a2d62be6a0`.

## Related

* KS-1256 (PR 2001's ticket); PR 2001 merged as `6a36d41b9852`.
* Board search before filing (team Secuura-PK, archived included): `api/admin/settings` 8 open (KS-485, KS-772, KS-1204, KS-1230, KS-1231, KS-1233, KS-1256, KS-1262), 0 closed; `api/verification/policy` 2 open (KS-736, KS-1256), 0 closed; `readPlatformSettings` 0 and 0; `PLATFORM_SETTINGS_DEFAULTS` 0 and 0. Control: `svc_gateway_settings` and `api/admin/settings` hit in the same run (2 and 8 open). KS-1256 names the two direct readers (above); KS-736 (mount-auth scoring) appears in the policy hits and this seat read its title only. This ticket is filed as its own ticket so that KS-1256 can close; the round trip with the changed PUT is not named in KS-1256.

title: Every read of svc_nft_certificates.public_fields runs JSON.parse on an already-parsed JSONB array, so a stored NFT certificate cannot be read back
description:
BLUF: In the nft-certificate service, every read of the `public_fields` column runs `JSON.parse` on a value the Postgres driver has already parsed. The column is JSONB, so the driver returns an array, `JSON.parse` of an array throws, and a stored certificate cannot be read back. The write path stores a JSON array, so this reaches every row the service writes itself. The rows are intact in the database; they are unreadable through the service. Priority High (the brief's suggestion, and my grade): the failure sits on the read path of every stored certificate, and nothing short of a code change works around it.

Source: /Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-04_seatW-27th/HANDOVER.md (lines 28 to 31) and /Volumes/DevMASTER/!CODING/Secuura/Blockchain/5_Project_History/2026-11-04_seatW-27th/evidence/search_nft_jsonb.out. Seat W 27th found it on a disposable stack (w27) at ee1e1b832115. I read the code at origin/develop 035685291b9d myself.

What I read (code, not a run):

* `Blockchain/Dev/migrations/002_verification-tiers.sql` line 796, inside `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS svc_nft_certificates` (line 784): `public_fields JSONB DEFAULT '[]'`. No other file under `Blockchain/Dev/migrations` names the column (searched `public_fields`).
* `Blockchain/Dev/services/nft-certificate/src/services/minting.service.ts` line 76 writes `JSON.stringify(cert.publicFields || [])` into that column.
* The same file reads it with `JSON.parse(row.public_fields || '[]')` at line 123 (`loadFromDb`, the startup load, which selects every row of `svc_nft_certificates`) and at lines 505, 592 and 678. The row type declares `public_fields: string`, which is not what a JSONB column returns.
* `loadFromDb` runs the parse inside its loop. The first row that holds an array makes it throw into the function's catch, so no later row is loaded.

What Seat W 27th measured on w27 (disposable stack, ee1e1b832115): the log lines `DB get user certificates failed` and `DB get wallet certificates failed`, each with `Unexpected end of JSON input`. A row whose `public_fields` is NULL reads fine.

Fix shape (not chosen here): accept the value the driver returns for JSONB (an array) at the four read sites, or make the column text and keep the stringify. Either needs a test that round-trips a stored row.

Not measured: a run of this code by me; how many rows `svc_nft_certificates` holds on kintsugi or the demo environment; whether any deployed environment overrides the driver's JSONB parser; what the three DB read paths return to the caller after the catch (W 27th's log lines are the only evidence of the failure itself).
Board search (this seat, 2026-11-05): `public_fields` 0 open and 0 closed literal hits; `minting.service` with `JSON.parse` 0; `Unexpected end of JSON input` 0. Seat W 27th named KS-1843 as the nearest neighbour, a different defect.

title: referral: duplicate milestone reward rows the re-award bug already stored stay stored and still count as pending rewards
description:
**BLUF:** The referral re-award bug (KS 1956) stored duplicate CLAIMABLE milestone reward rows in `svc_referral_milestones_rewards`: the same user and milestone, more than once. The repair in pull request 1979 stops NEW duplicates; it removes none. The rows already stored stay stored, and `GET /api/rewards/user` still counts every one of them as a pending reward that can be claimed. Any cleanup is a DATA change and Kam's decision later; this ticket proposes nothing destructive. Pre-existing, High (QA gate 162).

## What is measured

* **QA gate 162** (2026-11-03, real PostgreSQL 15, the real referral service over HTTP, on pull request 1979): before the repair the same user and milestone reached 2 to 4 rows across its cells. After the repair, new checks add none, and the progress row records each milestone once. Every duplicate row stored earlier is still there and is still a pending reward.
* **QA gate 153** (2026-11-03): `GET /api/rewards/user` shows these rows as pending with `canClaim: true`, which inflates the balance a user sees.

## What is not measured

* Whether production has `svc_referral_milestones_rewards` at all (the repo has no DDL for it, KS 1956), and if so how many duplicate rows it holds. Nothing in the repo shows production's schema or data.
