Project rule [KS-201](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-201/enforce-utc-for-all-datetime-handling-across-backend-services-and) requires every date to be UTC, so either answer is a defect to fix.

## Related

* [KS-1557](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-1557/security-a-write-role-caller-can-make-another-organisations-bytes): the read-side change (PR 1531) this suite pins.
* [KS-1474](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-1474/no-gate-executes-the-db-backed-integration-suites-the-default-test-run): no gate runs the DB-backed `*.integration.test.ts` suites, which is why a timezone-dependent red could go unnoticed.

## Not yet measured (filled in by the assignee or on request)

* The names of the 3 red cells.
* The pass/fail count for the same suite under `TZ=UTC`, to confirm the contrast.
* Whether the failing assertion is on a date value, a day boundary, or something else.

No fix is proposed here. Needs a Postgres for the integration suite (`npm run test:integration`).

title: Security: three certification write routes have NO per-record access check - POST /:id/verify, /:id/share and /:id/recertify, while /:id/revoke checks the issuer and /issue gates on a write role
description:
## BLUF

`POST /api/certifications/:id/verify`**,** `/:id/share` **and** `/:id/recertify` **carry no per-record access check.** They look a certification up by primary key and act on it. The only authorization on the path is the router-wide `authenticate()` plus tenant scoping, so **an authenticated caller in the same tenant** can reach a certification they are not a party to. The sibling write `POST /:id/revoke` **does** check (`certification.issuer.id !== issuer.id` -> 403), and `POST /issue` gates on a write role — so this is a gap between sibling routes in one file, not a missing convention.

Found while building the read bound for [KS-1695](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-1695) (PR #1667), by enumerating every by-id lookup in the file. **Facts only; no remedy proposed.** The read gap and this are the same class on different verbs.

## Measured at develop `7e3b9362e08b` (file: `Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/routes/certifications.ts`)

| route | opens | by-id lookup | `isAllowedByRoleOrScope` | `403` occurrences | per-record check |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `POST /issue` | `:180` | — | **1** (`:234`) | 5 | role/scope gate |
| `POST /:id/revoke` | `:1064` | `:1086` | 0 | **1** | **YES** — `issuer.id` mismatch -> 403 |
| `POST /:id/verify` | `:1139` | `:1150` | 0 | **0** | **NONE** |
| `POST /:id/share` | `:1209` | `:1232` | 0 | **0** | **NONE** |
| `POST /:id/recertify` | `:1310` | `:1332` | 0 | **0** | **NONE** |

**The whole file has exactly one router-level gate:** `certificationsRouter.use(authenticate())` at `:65` — authentication, no role term, no record term. `isAllowedByRoleOrScope` appears **twice in the file in total**: the import at `:48` and the single call at `:234` inside `POST /issue`.

**Instruments, and the control for each.**

* The per-route counts are a line-span census of each route's body. **Control: the counter is not stuck at zero** — the same census returns `isAllowedByRoleOrScope = 1` for `POST /issue` and `403 = 1` for `/:id/revoke`. An earlier run of this same census was discarded because a shell quoting fault made `sed` error and every count read `0` from empty input; the zeros above come from a run whose control fires.
* A body census cannot see a middleware gate, so **all four route headers were read directly.** Every middleware array holds only `express-validator` terms (`param`, `body`) — no rbac middleware on any of them.

**A claim in the file that this falsifies.** The comment above `:234` reads: *"KS-547 (KS-540 F-2): certification issuance gates like every other document-write verb — this was the one ungated write on the platform."* On the same router, three write verbs are ungated beyond authentication. Whatever was true when KS-547 shipped, "the one ungated write" does not describe this file now.

## What each route does once it is past the lookup

* `/:id/share` takes `recipients[].email` **from the caller** (validated as an email, `:1212-1217`) and creates share records for a certification the caller need not be a party to. It checks `status === 'revoked'` and nothing about who is asking.
* `/:id/recertify` mints a verification certificate against the original (`originalCert`, lookup `:1332`) and writes a `RECERTIFY` lineage event.
* `/:id/verify` reads and returns verification data; `getUserFromRequest` is not even consulted for a 401, unlike the other two.

## NOT measured — read this before acting on the table

* **None of these three routes was run.** There is no Docker on the host this was found on, so every row above is a source read at one sha, not an observed response. No status code in this ticket was returned by a server.
* **The audience is stated as "an authenticated caller in the same tenant", deliberately.** Gate BX1's measured phrase for the *read* routes — "every same-tenant user of any organisation" — is **not** carried over here, because nothing was executed against these routes and no reader role was tried. Whether a role incidentally blocks any of them is unverified.
* **Whether a share yields the sharer content they could not otherwise see is UNREAD.** `saveShare`, the share mailer, and the lineage share surface were not opened. The documents read admits a `recipientEmail`, and share delivery emails a link — either could matter, neither was followed.
* Whether `/:id/recertify`'s minted certificate is readable by, or attributed to, the caller: not traced.
* Tenant resolution uses `getReqTenantId`, which **falls back to a fixed default tenant** when `req.tenantId` is unset (`:107`, `DEFAULT_TENANT_ID`). What that means for these three routes specifically was not measured.
* **Not a duplicate, as far as a weak instrument can say.** `searchIssues` is unusable for counting here: a nonsense control term (`qqzz-control-term-no-such-thing-5417`) returned **12 hits, identical to every real term**. So candidates were read rather than counted. [KS-834](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-834) **is NOT this** — it concerns the **api-gateway's** mock verify route (`services/api-gateway/src/routes/verification.ts:556`) being mounted with no auth handler: a different file and a different route that shares the URL path. [KS-1664](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-1664) is recertify's anchor-before-write ordering, not access. Nothing was found covering share or recertify access — stated as "nothing found", not "nothing exists".

title: Security: GET /api/gdpr/deletion-log with no userId reads every tenant's deletion log — unfiltered SELECT on a table with no tenant_id, admitted to ORG_ADMIN
description:
**BLUF —** `GET /api/gdpr/deletion-log` **called with no** `userId` **runs an unfiltered** `SELECT` **over** `data_deletion_log`**, a table with no** `tenant_id` **column and no RLS policy, and the route admits** `ORG_ADMIN`**. So one organisation's admin can read the newest 100 deletion-log rows of every tenant on the deployment. Source-read on develop** `3a6f1810981e`**; NOT driven on a real Postgres as a second tenant's** `ORG_ADMIN` **— see Not measured.**

### The chain, with the instrument named for each count

| \# | fact | instrument |
| -- | -- | -- |
| 1 | the route is `gdprRouter.get('/deletion-log', requireRole('SYSTEM_ADMIN', 'ORG_ADMIN'), …)` and passes `req.query.userId` straight through | `routes/gdpr.ts:623-626`, read at develop `3a6f1810981e` |
| 2 | with no `userId`, the service runs `SELECT * FROM data_deletion_log ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100` — **no** `WHERE` **of any kind** | `services/gdprService.ts:1022-1034` |
| 3 | `data_deletion_log` has **no** `tenant_id` **column**: `id, user_id, dsr_id, data_type, records_affected, deletion_method, reason, performed_by, created_at` | `migrations/001_initial-schema.sql:473-483` |
| 4 | **no migration attaches an RLS policy to it** | `grep -rn "data_deletion_log" migrations/*.sql \| grep -iE "rls\|policy\|row level"` → 0 lines; the same grep without the second filter returns the two migrations that do touch it (`001`, `036`), so the instrument discriminates |
| 5 | the row reaches HTTP verbatim: `mapDeletionLogRow` copies `reason: r.reason` into `DeletionLogEntry.reason`, and `res.json({ success: true, logs })` returns it | `gdprService.ts:505-517`, `routes/gdpr.ts:627` |
| 6 | it is in the API contract | `originate.openapi.ts:2863`, `deletionLog: z.array(z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())).optional()` |
| 7 | only **4** non-test references to the table exist in the whole repo (2 `INSERT`, 2 `SELECT`) | `grep -rn "data_deletion_log" --include='*.ts' services packages`, minus `__tests__`; control token on the same instrument returns 0 |
| 8 | **no existing ticket covers this read** | census of **all 678** team issues, fetched paginated and matched locally: `data_deletion_log` appears in exactly one (KS-758, which names it only in its F9 prose); control term returns 0. `searchIssues` was **not** used to establish absence — it returns 12 hits for a deliberately meaningless term |

### What an `ORG_ADMIN` of tenant B therefore sees

Rows written for tenant A's subjects: the `data_type` erased, the `records_affected` count, `performed_by` (for connector erasures, `connector:<connectorId>` — a Platform-S organisation identifier), `created_at`, and `reason`. A `user_id` is present on the resolved-subject path, so tenant A's **user UUIDs** are in that payload too.

### Why it is filed now

It was found while censusing the readers of `reason` for KS-758 F9, which asks what the unresolvable connector-erasure path should record. The answer turned on this: anything written into `reason` is published on this endpoint, which is why KS-758's option (a) — the subject's `external_ref` as written — would put a Platform-S subject reference on a cross-tenant readable response. **That is evidence for KS-758's card, and the read itself is a separate defect from what KS-758 records**, so it is here rather than folded in.

### Not measured — stated plainly rather than implied

* **This is a source read.** The endpoint was **not** driven on a real Postgres while authenticated as a second tenant's `ORG_ADMIN`. Steps 1-6 are the code path; the exploit is inferred from them and has not been executed.
* **Whether a deployment actually has more than one tenant's rows in the table** is not measured here, and per-tenant database separation would change the blast radius. (The project's isolation model is per-tenant databases with RLS inert by construction — if that holds for every environment, the cross-tenant reach may be nil in practice and the defect is then the missing guard rather than a live exposure. Unverified either way by me.)
* `requireRole`**'s own semantics** — whether `ORG_ADMIN` is scoped to a tenant by the middleware before the handler runs — was not read. If it is, step 1 still permits the unfiltered query, because the handler applies no scope of its own.
* The resolved-subject path (`user_id` present) was not separately enumerated for how many such rows a real deployment holds.

### No remedy is proposed here

The shape of the fix is a design decision on a GDPR audit surface — add a tenant column and filter, scope by the caller's organisation, or restrict the route to `SYSTEM_ADMIN` — and each has a different effect on what an `ORG_ADMIN` can legitimately audit. It is ruled before it is built.

*Found 2026-10-20 by Seat G 13th while building KS-758 F9 (option (b)); develop* `3a6f1810981e3e268e77d0e4721987d186b71810`*.*

title: auth: a request in flight resurrects a revoked session — updateSessionActivity and rotateSessionRefreshToken write back the stale isActive:true record with a fresh 24h TTL (session.ts:270-294)
description:
## BLUF

**A revocation can be undone by any request that was already in flight.** `updateSessionActivity` (`session.ts:270-279`) and `rotateSessionRefreshToken` (`:282-294`) both do a read-modify-write: `get` the session JSON, mutate, `setex` it back. If `revokeSession` lands between the `get` and the `setex`, the **stale** `isActive:true` **record is written back with a fresh 24-hour TTL** — and the session is live again.

Worse, it becomes **unrevokable**: the revocation already removed it from `user_sessions:<id>`, so a later `revokeAllUserSessions` returns **0** and cannot find it.

Pre-existing. Filed from gate BO1's note N2 on PR #1655.

## Recommendation

Either a **revoked tombstone** that `getSession` checks, or a **conditional write** (a Lua script or a WATCH/MULTI compare-and-set) so a write cannot resurrect a record revoked since it was read. The tombstone is probably cheaper and also fixes the orphaned-from-the-set half.

## Why it matters more than a normal race

`updateSessionActivity` runs on **every authenticated request** (`middleware/authenticate.ts:160`), so the window is open continuously under load rather than at a rare moment. An attacker hammering requests on the old token widens it deliberately. It affects **every** revocation path — logout, the admin status change, user erasure, and the new password change/reset.

## The measurement (gate BO1, probe B3)

The interleave was forced deterministically:

* after the revocation (returned n=1, record inactive), the in-flight write left `getSession` returning the session **ACTIVE**;
* the session was already gone from `user_sessions:<id>`, so a second `revokeAllUserSessions` returned **0** and could not reach it.
* **Control B3c** — the same steps *without* the interleave: the session stayed revoked. So the probe measures the race, not a broken teardown.
* **Not run:** a timing measurement against real Redis. The probe drives the real `session.ts` against a fake that implements the session commands, so the *window's width* in production is unmeasured; its existence is not.

## Where

* `services/auth/src/services/session.ts:270-279` `updateSessionActivity`
* `services/auth/src/services/session.ts:282-294` `rotateSessionRefreshToken`
* called from `services/auth/src/middleware/authenticate.ts:160`

**Board search before filing:** `updateSessionActivity` returned **0** hits; `rotateSessionRefreshToken` returned 4, none about a resurrection race (KS-756 the opaque handle, KS-1687 m365 token persistence, KS-1150 the OAuth grant, KS-329 PQC); also searched "resurrect revoked session" and "session revoked refresh token still redeems". **Controls both ways:** a freshly generated never-published token returned **0**, `revokeAllUserSessions` returned **1**.

Related KS-1407.

title: auth: the OAuth refresh_token grant never checks the ORIGIN SESSION, so a revoked session's refresh token still redeems and mints a brand-new session (oauth.ts:988-1089)
description:
## BLUF

`POST /api/oauth/token` **with** `grant_type=refresh_token` **never reads** `decoded.sessionId`**, so revoking a user's sessions does not reach the OAuth refresh path.** A refresh token issued before a revocation still redeems, and mints a *brand-new* session. Measured by the gate on PR #1655 (KS-1407): after `revokeAllUserSessions` (n=1, `getSession` null), the same refresh token redeemed **200**, then **200 again**, leaving the account with **2 live sessions**.

Pre-existing; **outside** that PR's diff. Filed from gate BO1's note N1.

## Recommendation

Check the origin session on this grant (or introduce a per-user credential epoch) before minting. The oracle is already in the repo: the *interactive* `POST /api/auth/refresh` does a server-side session lookup at `routes/auth.ts:688-689`, so the two refresh paths disagree about whether a session must still exist. Wednesday or Kam should rule whether the fix rides with a KS-1407 follow-up or stands alone.

## Where

`services/auth/src/routes/oauth.ts:988-1089` — the `grant_type=refresh_token` branch. It verifies the JWT, checks the jti denylist, pins `user.status === 'ACTIVE'` at `:1067`, and mints a new session at `:1078`. It never consults the session named by the token it is redeeming.

## The measurement (gate BO1, probe C1)

Real `session.ts`, real `refreshDenylist.ts`, real `jwt.ts`, on the ks823 scaffold:

1. created a session and minted an OAuth pair bound to public client `pub-1`;
2. ran `revokeAllUserSessions` — returned n=1, and `getSession` then returned null;
3. redeemed the same refresh token: **200**. Redeemed again: **200**. Account left with **2 live sessions**.

* **Control in the same case:** a client-mismatch redeem was refused **400**, so the harness can produce a refusal.
* **Not run:** an authorization code issued before a revocation and exchanged after it. The code grant also mints a fresh session (`:969`), so it is plausibly a smaller sibling — unmeasured, stated as such.

## Consequence

Anyone holding an OAuth grant obtained before a password change, a password reset, an admin status change or a user erasure keeps a renewable foothold. It is the direct counterexample to KS-1407's premise that no session may outlive the password that minted it.

## Scope — what this ticket is NOT

**KS-1150 R-2 already covers the rotation/denylist half of this branch** ("the refresh grant does not rotate / denylist the presented token", `:836`/`:860`) and is still OPEN — its 2026-09-14 comment records R-1 landing as `b42e260c9897` with "R-2 / R-3 stay OPEN". **This ticket is the other half: the missing ORIGIN-SESSION check.** They are overlapping-but-distinct, not duplicates — a perfectly rotating implementation would still mint a new session for an account whose sessions were all revoked, because nothing reads `decoded.sessionId`. Do not close either as a duplicate of the other.

**Board search before filing:** `revokeAllUserSessions`, `updateSessionActivity`, `rotateSessionRefreshToken`, `decoded.sessionId`, "oauth refresh token revoked session", "session revoked refresh token still redeems". Nearest neighbours KS-1150 (the rotation half, above), KS-756 (the opaque session refresh handle, a different mechanism), KS-1280 (a revoked session's Bearer forwarded by originate, a different service). **Controls both ways:** a freshly generated token that was never published returned **0** hits, and `revokeAllUserSessions` returned **1** — so the search discriminates.

Related KS-1407, KS-1150.

title: Security: POST /api/documents/:id/version has NO per-document access check on its source - any write-role caller in the tenant can derive a new version from another organisation's document (the sibling of the certify path KS-1557/#1619 closed)
description:
## BLUF

`POST /api/documents/:id/version` **checks a ROLE, a SCOPE and the TENANT, and nothing about the caller's relationship to the source document.** Any write-role caller in the tenant can derive a new version from **another organisation's** document, and the derived row is a real child of it. This is the sibling of the path KS-1557 / pull request #1619 closed on `POST /api/certifications/issue`: the same defect class, the same service, still open on the versioning route. Measured on a scratch stack at develop `89956fe92956`. Facts only — no fix is proposed here.

## Where

`services/originate/src/routes/documents.ts`, the `'/:id/version'` handler:

* `:2219` — `const ALLOWED_VERSION_ROLES = DOCUMENT_WRITE_ROLES;`
* `:2246` — `isAllowedByRoleOrScope(req, ALLOWED_VERSION_ROLES, 'documents:write')` — role or scope only.
* `:2281` — `const source = await getDocument(id, tenantId, (req as any).db);` followed by a 404 when it does not resolve, and a `metadata.documentType` guard. **There is no owner / recipient / creating-connector test anywhere in the handler** — the check `callerMayCertifyDocument` applies on the certify path (`routes/certifications.ts:119-128`, call sites `:223` legacy and `:441` lineage) has no counterpart here.

## Measured (scratch Postgres 15 at migration 054, real `documents` + `certifications` routers, `secuura_app`, both `MULTI_TENANCY_ENABLED=false` and `=true` — identical results in both)

| cell | what was done | result |
| -- | -- | -- |
| G1 | **a FOREIGN organisation's connector** calls `/version` on organisation A's document | **201.** The minted row is a real child: its `parent_document_id` resolves to A's document. |
| G1 (same cell) | **the discriminating control** — that **same caller**, on that **same document**, through `POST /api/certifications/issue` with `parentDocumentId` | **403** `FORBIDDEN` |
| G2 | an **interactive write-role USER of another organisation** calls `/version` on A's document | **201** |
| G3 | **the bound** — a caller in **another tenant** calls `/version` on A's document | **404** `NOT_FOUND "Document not found in this tenant"` |

G1's two halves are the finding in one line: **the two sibling routes disagree about the same caller on the same document.** G3 bounds it — it does not cross the tenant, because `getDocument` is tenant-scoped.

## Board search before filing (symbol and path, each with a control)

* `callerMayCertifyDocument` → **2** hits (KS-1557, KS-1679); `isAllowedByRoleOrScope` → **2** (KS-1202, KS-1433). Both controls fire, so the instrument discriminates rather than returning everything.
* `ALLOWED_VERSION_ROLES`, `/:id/version`, `documents/:id/version`, `parent_document_id` → each returns the 12-hit fuzzy cap, and **none of the hits names this defect.** The nearest four, each a different thing: **KS-1538** (the legacy certify path — fixed), **KS-1557** (the lineage certify path — this route's sibling), **KS-1508** (`versionedById` is server-set — same route, different defect), **KS-1228** (a refused request still writes an `action_provenance` row — same route, different defect).
* **0 open hits for the source-access check itself.**

## Sequencing — this matters before anyone gates this route

The KS-1557 fix (shape (a′): `/version` records the creating connector on the document it mints, under the action value `create:connector`) **must land before any source-access gate is added here.** Otherwise a gate written with the same predicate would refuse `/version` on a version-minted document for exactly the reason certify refuses it today: a `/version`-created document has no creation provenance row of its own, so `wasCreatedByConnector` is false for the connector that actually made it. Measured on demo: **31 of 31** `/version`-minted documents have no such row.

## Open question, UNMEASURABLE from this project

**Does Platform S ever version a document it did not itself originate?** It decides the client-visible risk of closing this gap — if S does, closing it turns some S calls into 403. It cannot be answered from here: `Secuura/platform-s` returns 404 to this project's PAT (which sees exactly one repository), so no search of S's code is possible from Platform K's identity. **Stated as a question, not an assumption, and not asked of anyone here.**

## Not claimed

* No severity judgement beyond the priority on this ticket, and no fix design.
* The derived row carries the **caller's own** `newContentHash`, so this is not an alteration of the source document's bytes; the source gains a child it did not consent to, and the derived row presents as part of its lineage.
* Not measured: whether any such cross-organisation version exists in live data.

Found by Seat C 31st while measuring KS-1557 (Stuart's comment `16e8498d`) at develop `89956fe92956`, 2026-10-20.

title: A fresh clone has no pre-push gate: core.hooksPath is unset, so the 16-leg preflight silently does not run
description:
**BLUF: a working copy cloned from GitHub has NO pre-push gate.** `core.hooksPath` **is unset in a fresh clone,** `.git/hooks/pre-push` **does not exist there, so the 16-leg preflight does not run — silently. The push just succeeds. A worktree off the shared checkout inherits the gate; a clone does not.**

## Measured 2026-10-19, read-only `git config --get core.hooksPath`

| working copy | `core.hooksPath` | gate runs? |
| -- | -- | -- |
| the shared checkout `2_Project_Files` | `.githooks` | yes |
| a worktree off it (`worktrees/s-r46-ks1462`) | `.githooks` (inherited) | yes |
| a fresh `git clone` from GitHub | **UNSET** | **NO** |
| `deploy-clones/seatC25-7e2f8157cec2` (a live seat's clone at the time) | **UNSET** | **NO** |

`.githooks/pre-push` is present and executable in the clone — it is simply never invoked, because nothing points git at it.

## Why this is worth a ticket rather than a note

**The failure is silent and it looks like success.** A push from an unwired clone prints no warning and no leg output; it prints the ordinary "new branch" line. There is nothing in the output that says the gate was skipped, so the only way to notice is to know the leg headers should be there and see that they are not.

**It happened, on this ticket's own session.** Seat E 3rd's first push of the KS-1195 branch ran with no gate. It was rejected by the remote for an unrelated reason — the branch name collided with a stale 17-September branch — so nothing landed and no ungated commit exists. Had the name been free, an ungated push would have succeeded and been reported as pushed. That is luck, not a control.

**It is already documented**, at `Blockchain/Dev/CONTRIBUTING.md:389`:
`git config core.hooksPath .githooks && chmod +x .githooks/pre-push`
So this is a missable step, not an undocumented hole. The problem is that missing it is undetectable from the push's own output.

## Fix shapes (not chosen here)

1. **Make the absence loud rather than the wiring mandatory.** A tracked `Blockchain/Dev/scripts/*` check, or a preflight leg, that refuses when `core.hooksPath` does not resolve to `.githooks` — this cannot help the very push it would gate, so it only helps on the *second* push onward.
2. **A** `postinstall` **/ bootstrap step** that sets `core.hooksPath` when it is unset. `npm ci` is `ignore-scripts` in this repo, so a postinstall would not fire; it would have to hang off an existing bootstrap script the seats already run.
3. **Have the launcher wire it for every working copy it knows about**, including `deploy-clones/*`, rather than relying on the clone inheriting anything.
4. **A server-side ruleset** that refuses a push without the evidence the hook produces. The strongest, and the most work; also note "Require status checks" must never be enabled while Actions are retired, so this would need to be something other than a check.

Shape 1 or 3 looks like the cheapest honest improvement; the decision is not mine.

## Reproduce

```
git clone --single-branch --branch develop git@github.com:Secuura/Distributed_Secuura.git /tmp/probe
git -C /tmp/probe config --get core.hooksPath   # prints nothing, exit 1
ls /tmp/probe/.git/hooks/pre-push               # No such file or directory
```

Discovered 2026-10-19 by Seat E 3rd during the KS-1195 build (PR #1613), after the push log showed zero leg output.

title: Chain-first verify blobs hard-code `anchored: true` and drop anchoring's status/acknowledged, so a 'submitting' or failed anchor reads isAnchored: true (v1 + v2)
description:
## BLUF

**The chain-first verify branches build their blockchain blob with** `anchored: true` **hard-coded and no** `status`**, which makes the honest-anchor guard** `settled` **BY CONSTRUCTION.** An anchoring reply that is still in flight or has failed — `status: 'submitting'`, `acknowledged: false`, the KS-726 class — is therefore presented as `isAnchored: true`, in both the v1 and the v2 verify routes.

The code says so itself. `services/originate/src/routes/verification.ts:130-132`:

> *"KS-1628: a failed anchor is not an anchor, whatever else the blob says. The chain-first blobs carry* `anchored: true` *and no status, so they are unaffected; a stored blob that pairs* `anchored: true` *with a failed status was on-chain before this line."*

That comment reads as a reassurance. It is in fact the statement of the defect: *unaffected by the failed-status guard* is exactly the problem, because the guard is the thing that would have caught this.

Gate O1's Minor 2 on the twelve-PR batch, 2026-10-19T01:00:25Z. Pre-existing; not in those merges.

## The mechanism, measured

`isAnchoredHonestly` (`verification.ts:120`) decides the claim:

```ts
if (FAILED_ANCHOR_STATUSES.has(String(c.status))) return false;   // :133
const settled = c.anchored === true || c.status === 'confirmed';  // :141
```

* A **real stored** anchor row has no `anchored` boolean at all — the comment at `:136-139` says so: *"anchoring's vocabulary is pending | submitted | confirmed | failed … and there is NO* `anchored` *boolean on a real row."* For those rows only `status === 'confirmed'` earns the claim, and `'submitted'` deliberately does not, because *"the tx is in flight and may still fail — the KS-535 class."*
* A **chain-first** blob is built by hand with `anchored: true` and **no** `status` **key**. So `FAILED_ANCHOR_STATUSES.has(String(undefined))` is false — the failed guard cannot fire — and `settled` is true on the first disjunct, whatever anchoring actually reported.

**The four construction sites:**

| route | site |
| -- | -- |
| v1 | `services/originate/src/routes/verification.ts:717` |
| v1 | `services/originate/src/routes/verification.ts:1237` |
| v1 | `services/originate/src/routes/verification.ts:1259` |
| **v2** | `services/originate/src/routes/verificationV2.ts:233`, inside `chainOnlyMatch` |

The `status` argument the call sites pass does not rescue it: `verification.ts:758`, `:1297` and `verificationV2.ts:271` pass the **literal** `'anchored'`, and in any case the second argument is only consulted when there is no chain blob at all (`:149`).

**What bounds the severity.** `settled` is necessary but not sufficient: the claim also needs `typeof c.txHash === 'string'`, `REAL_TXHASH_RE` (64 hex) and `heightOk`. So the hash must already look like a real one, and it comes from the chain index. The defect is that **in-flight and failed anchors the index knows about still read as anchored** — not that an arbitrary blob does.

## Why High

On a document-authenticity platform, `isAnchored: true` is the product's central claim to a verifier. Presenting a `'submitting'` or failed anchor as anchored is the same family as KS-535 (a failed on-chain anchor reporting `status: anchored`) and KS-1634 (a simulated anchor returned unlabelled), and KS-1634 is High. The failure direction is always *over*-claiming, never under-claiming.

**Honest limit on this rating: I did not run a census.** I have not measured how many rows can reach these branches with a non-confirmed status today. The nearest evidence is KS-1634's census — 0 qualifying rows on both boxes at 2026-10-18, with kintsugi's 0 noted as contingent on one document row — and that census was for a different precondition. **A census is the first step on this ticket, and the rating should be revisited against it.**

## Recommendation

1. Carry anchoring's own fields into the chain-first blob instead of asserting the conclusion: pass `status` and `acknowledged` through, and let `isAnchoredHonestly` apply the same rules it applies to a stored row. Dropping `anchored: true` entirely is the cleaner shape, since no real row carries it — but `ks563` pins the current chain-first shape, so that is a deliberate change with a test to re-cut, not a one-liner.
2. A cell per site: a chain-first match whose anchoring status is `'submitting'` (and one that is `'failed'`) must read `isAnchored: false`. A mutant restoring the hard-coded `anchored: true` must red each of them.
3. Fold the **v2** site in with KS-1634's v2 work — it is the same four lines of construction, and splitting them across two tickets invites one to be done and the other forgotten.

## Dedupe

Over all **1,627** Secuura-PK issues including archived: `chainOnlyMatch` **→ 0 hits.** `anchored: true` → 4, each a different subject (KS-1634 the simulated-label defect, KS-1628 the route retirement, KS-834 a decision on verify auth, KS-535 the document-status variant, Done). `acknowledged` → 6, none about this presenter. `isAnchored` → 9; the nearest, KS-1637, is gate N1's residue about the removal pin reading only the router — a different mechanism, read and confirmed distinct. Positive controls on the same corpus: `verification` 360, `anchor` 313. Zero control: a nonsense token reads 0.

**Related:** KS-1634 (the same presenter, the `simulated` signal, and the v2 site it shares), KS-726 (the `status: 'submitting'` / `acknowledged: false` reply class this mis-presents; Done), KS-535 (the document-status variant; Done), KS-563 (which pins the current chain-first shape, so its cells are in scope for any change here).

---

*Filed by Seat R 51st on Wednesday's instruction of 2026-10-19T01:00:25Z, citing gate O1's verdict section "Minor 2". The Linear actor field is shared across the fleet, so authorship is this line, not the actor. Everything above the "Why High" section I verified in the source at develop* `37834600a543cb0276f427d969ac034d9df74fbd`*; the severity and the census limit are my own call, stated as such. Not fixed in these merges.*

title: GET /api/keys has no organisation arm: an ORG_ADMIN or ISSUER_ADMIN lists another organisation's keys in the same tenant
description:
## BLUF

`GET /api/keys` **has no organisation arm.** An `ORG_ADMIN` or `ISSUER_ADMIN` of organisation A lists organisation B's API keys when B is in the same tenant, using B's exact id. The mint and the revoke are both organisation-bounded for these roles; the list is the only one of the three routes that is not. **Measured** at develop `7c6b3d88`, details below. Facts only, no fix. Filed on Wednesday's ruling while building KS-1553 PR 1, which does **not** add the bound.

**What is exposed:** each key's **id, name, prefix, scopes and connector id**, plus `lastUsedAt`, `usageCount`, `isActive` and `createdAt`. **Not key material:** the list never returns the key or its hash.

**Not reached by Kam's ADMIN ruling.** That ruling (KS-1570) concerns the tenant-level `ADMIN` role on the mint. The roles here are `ORG_ADMIN` and `ISSUER_ADMIN`, which are organisation-bounded on the mint (KS-1533) and on the revoke (KS-764).

## The code

At develop `7c6b3d88`, `services/security/src/index.ts:1318-1366`:

* The handler filters `k.organizationId === organizationId`, where `organizationId` is the raw query value, and then `callerIsPlatform || k.tenantId === caller.tenantId`. That second filter is KS-742's tenant bound.
* Nothing in the handler reads `caller.organizationId` or calls `isOrgBoundedRole`.
* The mint, by contrast, calls `decideTenantAccess(user, tenantId, { targetOrganizationId })` (`index.ts:1173`). That engages the organisation arm for `ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES = {ORG_ADMIN, ISSUER_ADMIN}` (`packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts`).
* The revoke is bounded by `decideKeyRevoke` (KS-764).

## Measured

A throwaway in-process probe, using the same harness as `ks1533-key-mint-organisation-arm.test.ts` (memory-backed; the list reads only `memApiKeys`). Organisation ids contain hex letters, so the upper-case form is not identical to the original.

| caller | lists | result |
| -- | -- | -- |
| platform (`super_admin`) | mints for A1 and A2 | 201, 201 |
| `ISSUER_ADMIN` of A1 | A1 | 200, 1 key |
| `ISSUER_ADMIN` **of A1** | **A2, exact id** | **200, 1 key (the gap)** |
| `ISSUER_ADMIN` of A1 | A2, upper-case | 200, 0 keys (only because the compare is raw; see below) |
| CONTROL: `ISSUER_ADMIN` of a tenant-B org | A2 | 200, 0 keys (the tenant filter is real) |
| CONTROL: platform | A2 | 200, 1 key |

**After KS-1553 PR 1** the list normalises the query, so the upper-case form of A2 also lists A2's key. That reveals nothing the exact id does not already reveal. PR 1 pins both as cells labelled MEASURED GAP that name this ticket, so adding a bound later is a visible edit.

## Dedupe

I scanned all 1,560 issues, archived ones included, with their comments, for list / another-organisation / organisation-arm wording. The positive control (KS-1533 matching "organisation arm") fired, and a bogus-symbol control returned 0. Nothing covers the list. KS-742 bounded the list by **tenant** only.

## Not decided here

The shape of the bound: refuse, or filter as KS-742 and `GET /api/audit` do. Also how it treats the org-less bounded accounts KS-779 recorded as intentional.

title: POLICY (Kam's call): role ADMIN is a KEY_ADMIN_ROLE that the KS-764 organisation arm never engages for, so a tenant ADMIN can mint a key for any organisation in its tenant
description:
## BLUF

`ADMIN` **is in** `KEY_ADMIN_ROLES` **but in neither** `PLATFORM_ROLES` **nor** `ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES`**, so the KS-764 organisation arm is skipped for it entirely and** `decideTenantAccess` **falls through to** `allow: 'same-tenant'`**.** After KS-1533 arm 1 closes the hole for `ORG_ADMIN` and `ISSUER_ADMIN`, a caller with role `ADMIN` can **still** mint a key carrying any organisation's `organizationId` inside its own tenant — the same Path 1 shape, through one role.

**This is a policy question about who may reach an irreversible cross-organisation erasure, so it is Kam's to decide, not an engineering choice inside a PR.** Wednesday put it on his board as a card (`secuura-ks1533-admin-role-unbounded-by-org-arm-1013`) and recommended leaving `ADMIN` unbounded. **Until he rules, KS-1533 arm 1 ships leaving** `ADMIN` **unbounded and says so plainly**, and the shared role set is NOT touched.

## The three sets, read at source

```
KEY_ADMIN_ROLES    services/security/src/provisioningPolicy.ts:43-49
                   SYSTEM_ADMIN, SUPER_ADMIN, ORG_ADMIN, ISSUER_ADMIN, ADMIN
PLATFORM_ROLES     packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts:59
                   SYSTEM_ADMIN, SUPER_ADMIN
ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES  packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts:76
                   ORG_ADMIN, ISSUER_ADMIN
```

The arm is `if (organisationScope && isOrgBoundedRole(user.role))` (`keyRevokePolicy.ts:173`). `ADMIN` satisfies neither predicate, so the arm is skipped and the function returns `allow: 'same-tenant'` at `:225`.

| role | what arm 1 does for it |
| -- | -- |
| `SYSTEM_ADMIN`, `SUPER_ADMIN` | platform — bypass the arm by design (KS-577 depends on it) |
| `ORG_ADMIN`, `ISSUER_ADMIN` | org-bounded — **the arm applies**, which is KS-1533 arm 1 |
| `ADMIN` | **neither — the arm never engages** |

## The two readings

**(a) By design, and this ticket closes as "documented".** `ADMIN` reads as a **tenant**-level admin, distinct from platform — KS-1283 is about "a widened `SUPER_ROLES` would admit a tenant `ADMIN` role on six routes", which treats it as a tenant role. On that reading, acting across organisations *inside its own tenant* is what a tenant admin is for, and arm 1 is complete as scoped.

**(b) A gap.** The sink is the KS-695 connector erasure, which is **irreversible** and destroys another organisation's titles, descriptions and name. KS-764's stated hazard is "an org-bounded admin in organisation A destroying organisation B's key" — if a tenant `ADMIN` may do the equivalent to B's *documents*, the boundary is only as strong as the weakest admin role.

**This ticket does not pick.** It records the question, the evidence, and what shipped in the meantime.

## If Kam rules (b)

`ADMIN` joins `ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES` in `packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts`. That is a **one-line change to a shared set that also governs the revoke route**, so it is not a local edit: it would change `DELETE /api/security/keys/:id` for every `ADMIN` caller too, and it needs its own gate and its own caller-population check (the same `caller has no organisation` 403 that KS-1533 arm 1 accepts for org-bounded roles would then apply to `ADMIN` as well). It should not be folded into KS-1533.

## Where it is pinned meanwhile

KS-1533 arm 1 carries a **documenting cell** that asserts today's behaviour — a tenant `ADMIN` minting for another organisation in its tenant succeeds — labelled as undecided policy rather than as a guarantee, so that whichever way Kam rules, the change is visible as a deliberate edit to a cell rather than a silent flip.

## Dedupe

Literal, case-insensitive over title and description, archived included: `ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES` **1** (KS-779 — the CALLER-side population of org-bounded accounts with no organisation claim, which is KS-1533 arm 1's accepted 403 price, not this question), `isOrgBoundedRole` **0**, `tenant ADMIN` 4 and `ADMIN role` 6 (the KS-1283 / KS-1506 / KS-486 family — a widened `SUPER_ROLES`, error-handler and review tickets, none of them this question). KS-764 (Done) created the arm and deliberately scoped it to the revoke route.

*Corrected after filing: the first version of this paragraph said* `ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES` *0. The scan returned KS-779. The conclusion is unchanged — no ticket asks whether* `ADMIN` *should be org-bounded — but the figure was wrong and a wrong dedupe count is worth correcting rather than leaving.*

Raised by Seat V 5th while building KS-1533 arm 1, 2026-10-12. Found by reading the role sets before writing the fix, not by a test.

---

## ADDENDUM — it is TWO roles, not one, and the verdicts are MEASURED by running the predicates

I ran the real `isPlatformRole`, `isOrgBoundedRole` and `decideTenantAccess` over the whole role vocabulary rather than reading the sets. Caller is `{role, tenantId:'t1', organizationId:'oA'}`, target is the same tenant and a DIFFERENT organisation `oB` — i.e. exactly the KS-1533 Path 1 shape:

| role (as the JWT carries it) | isPlatformRole | isOrgBoundedRole | verdict naming ANOTHER org in the same tenant |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `SYSTEM_ADMIN` | true | false | ALLOW `platform-admin` — by design |
| `SUPER_ADMIN` | true | false | ALLOW `platform-admin` — by design |
| `super_admin` | true | false | ALLOW `platform-admin` — by design |
| `platform_admin` | **false** | **false** | **ALLOW** `same-tenant` **— UNBOUNDED** |
| `PLATFORM_ADMIN` | **false** | **false** | **ALLOW** `same-tenant` **— UNBOUNDED** |
| `ADMIN` | **false** | **false** | **ALLOW** `same-tenant` **— UNBOUNDED** |
| `admin` | **false** | **false** | **ALLOW** `same-tenant` **— UNBOUNDED** |
| `ORG_ADMIN` | false | true | DENY `cross-organisation` — arm 1 working |
| `ISSUER_ADMIN` | false | true | DENY `cross-organisation` — arm 1 working |
| `issuer_admin` | false | true | DENY `cross-organisation` — arm 1 working |
| `connector` | false | false | ALLOW `same-tenant` — correct: `decideMint` pins a provisioner to its own tenant on its own branch |

Both predicates upper-case the claim (`keyRevokePolicy.ts:84` and `:123`), so casing is NOT the issue — the role simply is not in either set.

### `platform_admin` is the more interesting half

`platform_admin` is treated as a **super-role by the gateway** in at least six places, while the key policy does not treat it as platform at all:

```
services/api-gateway/src/routes/platform.ts:65      SUPER_ROLES          includes platform_admin
services/api-gateway/src/middleware/auth.ts:515     SUPER_ADMIN_ROLES    includes platform_admin
services/api-gateway/src/routes/admin.ts:577        PLATFORM_SCOPE_ROLES includes platform_admin
services/api-gateway/src/routes/proxy.ts:1094,1227                       include platform_admin
services/api-gateway/src/routes/audit-export.ts:105 adminRoles           includes platform_admin
packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts:59  PLATFORM_ROLES       does NOT
services/auth/src/routes/users.ts:193               PLATFORM_ADMIN_ROLES does NOT (it has `admin` instead)
```

So a `platform_admin` is "platform" to the gateway and an ordinary tenant user to the key policy. For arm 1 that means **unbounded**; more generally it is a role-vocabulary split across seven divergent lists, which is its own problem and not this ticket's to fix.

### What this changes for Kam's decision

The card is about who may reach an irreversible cross-organisation erasure. The answer is not "ADMIN" but "`ADMIN` **and** `platform_admin`**, in either casing**". If Kam rules them bounded, the edit is to `ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES` (or to `PLATFORM_ROLES`, for `platform_admin`) — still a shared set that governs the revoke route too, so still not a local change and still its own gate.

KS-1533 arm 1's documenting cell therefore pins **both** roles' current behaviour, labelled as undecided policy.

*Added by Seat V 5th, 2026-10-12, after running the predicates while building KS-1533 arm 1.*

---

## ⚠ CORRECTION — `platform_admin` is NOT unbounded at the mint. It cannot mint at all. Only `ADMIN` is the open question.

**The addendum above is wrong about** `platform_admin`**, and the retitle that named it was wrong.** Measured on the running security service over real HTTP while writing KS-1533 PR A's cells, and confirmed by running the function:

```
role              decideMint (runs FIRST, as route middleware)
ADMIN / admin     ALLOW via admin   -> reaches decideTenantAccess -> unbounded   (the claim HOLDS)
platform_admin    DENY 403 "API key management requires an admin role"          (the claim was WRONG)
PLATFORM_ADMIN    DENY 403 — same
ISSUER_ADMIN      ALLOW via admin   -> the organisation arm applies
super_admin       ALLOW via admin   -> platform, bypasses by design
```

**What I got wrong, precisely.** I ran `decideTenantAccess` on its own and concluded `platform_admin` falls through to `allow: 'same-tenant'`. That is true *of that function*. But the mint route runs `requireKeyAdminOrProvisioner` → `decideMint` **first**, and `PLATFORM_ADMIN` is not in `KEY_ADMIN_ROLES` (`provisioningPolicy.ts:43-49`), so the request is refused 403 before `decideTenantAccess` is ever called. **Order is invisible to a function call** — the exact point KS-742's route-contract test makes in its header, and that I copied into KS-1533's. The real-HTTP cell is what caught it: I had written it to assert `platform_admin` mints (201), and it read 403 on the unfixed service.

**So, for Kam's decision:** the question is `ADMIN` **only**. `ADMIN` is in `KEY_ADMIN_ROLES`, passes `decideMint`, reaches `decideTenantAccess`, and — being in neither `PLATFORM_ROLES` nor `ORG_BOUNDED_ROLES` — keeps cross-organisation mint inside its tenant. That half stands and is unchanged.

**What still stands about** `platform_admin`**:** the role-vocabulary split (KS-1536) is real — the gateway treats it as a super-role in six places. But its consequence *at the mint* is the opposite of what I wrote: a gateway super-role is **over**-restricted here (cannot mint keys), not under-restricted. That is an availability quirk, not a security hole, and it belongs on KS-1536, not on Kam's policy card.

The title is reverted to name `ADMIN` alone. KS-1533 PR A pins both facts in cells: `ADMIN` as UNDECIDED POLICY (201 today), `platform_admin` as MEASURED (403, refused by `decideMint`).

*Corrected by Seat V 5th, 2026-10-12. The third time this session I have had to correct a claim of mine in place; this one was on Kam's board, so it matters more than the dedupe counts did.*

title: Timestamping: the opentimestamps and blockchain types still report verified true, and /verify accepts a forged proof with no stored row (KS-753 gate m2)
description:
**ACTION (owner: the timestamping build lane, with a policy decision first):** decide what an `opentimestamps` or `blockchain` timestamp may claim when nothing external ever checked it, then make creation and `/api/timestamps/verify` agree with that decision, the way KS-753 and KS-1404 did for `rfc3161`. Options to rule between: (a) report `verified: false` on creation and on verify for these two types until a real attestation check exists; (b) require a stored row and honour its `verified` column on verify (KS-1404's shape for rfc3161); (c) stop advertising the types in `supportedTypes` (`index.ts:185`) until they are real. Tests first, with a planted-red mutation per branch.

**Symptom (gate evidence P7, P8).**

* **P7:** creating an `opentimestamps` or `blockchain` timestamp answers `verified: true` and persists `verified = true`. Both types are placeholders by design (the proof is generated locally, `generateMockOpenTimestampsProof` / blockchain at `index.ts:689` and `:705`).
* **P8:** a **forged** `opentimestamps` JSON proof (the right hash plus one attestation) with **no stored row** returns `verified: true` from `/verify` (`index.ts:616-621`; the `blockchain` case at `:625` is the same shape: hash match plus `chain` and `slot` fields). Nothing checks an attestation against anything.
* KS-1404 closed this same forgery path for `rfc3161` only.

**Why P2.** This is "a mock timestamp reported as verified" by KS-753's own wording, on an evidentiary path (Tier 1). It is **not a regression** from PR #1502 and did not block it; the PR declared these types out of scope.

**Data, handled separately.** Rows of these types already stored as `verified = true` are a data question. A backfill is approval-class (Kam), and the count must come first, read-only per environment, classified by the proof's SHAPE rather than the `(mock)` name (the name missed 1 of 5 mocks in the gate's test). Wednesday is handing the count SQL to the deploy seat.

Source: the Opus QA gate of PR #1502 (KS-753), verdict sha256/16 `5e1fcf87edc4e8a4`, finding m2. Wednesday ruled on 2026-10-12 (12:20Z) that this is filed as P2. PR #1502 head `5daf8830dc46`; line numbers below are at that head.

title: Wallet login: a suspended account stored under a mixed-case address can be evaded by logging in with the lower-case form (needs a case-insensitive lookup, a migration)
description:
## BLUF

Residual declared on #1476 (KS-806) and confirmed by its Opus delta gate (round 3), filed at the priority Wednesday asked for. A wallet account whose `wallet_address` was stored before #1476 in a NON-canonical casing and has since been SUSPENDED refuses its own casing (401), but the same wallet logging in with the lower-case form gets a NEW ACTIVE account (200). Suspension can be evaded through the double-account path.

## Recommendation

A separate PR with a migration: replace `auth_find_user_by_wallet` (migration 039, exact equality) with a case-insensitive lookup (or add a functional index on `lower(wallet_address)` and look up on the lower-cased argument), and canonicalise the stored column for existing rows in the same migration. Then the lookup in `routes/wallet.ts` needs no presented-casing-first loop. Until then #1476's raw-casing-first lookup keeps a legacy row reachable by its own casing, which is the part it can fix without a migration.

## Detail

* **Why it exists:** CIP-8 verification compares the claimed and signed address case-insensitively (`utils/cip8.ts`), so one wallet can present several casings, but `auth_find_user_by_wallet` is `WHERE wallet_address = p_wallet_address` (exact). #1476 stores new rows in the canonical lower-case form and looks up the presented casing first, then the canonical form; a legacy row in a casing the wallet does not present is not found by any lookup there.
* **Effect (gate probe D5 and the residual cell):** legacy row `L` (mixed case, SUSPENDED). Login with the mixed-case form: 401 (the suspension holds). Login with the lower-case form: no row found, a new row `N` is created, ACTIVE, 200.
* **Related, declared in #1476:** `/link` stores the raw casing (`routes/wallet.ts`), so one wallet can also become two accounts there; `/status/:walletAddress` is not canonicalised. The same migration fixes the lookup side of both; the write side of `/link` should canonicalise.
* **Not caused by #1476:** before it, every casing was a separate account anyway; #1476 closes the double account for rows it creates and leaves this one for legacy rows.

Provenance: Opus delta gate on #1476 round 3, verdict `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1476-r3/verdict.md`; filed by Seat V 3rd on Wednesday's instruction. Related: KS-806, KS-1486 (concurrent first logins), KS-1460.

title: Wallet login: two simultaneous first logins for one address issue a token for an id that is not in the database (4 of 5 rounds)
description:
## BLUF

Pre-existing on develop, found by the Opus gate on #1476 (KS-806) and filed at the priority Wednesday asked for. Two concurrent FIRST wallet logins for the same address both succeed with 200, only one row is created, and in 4 of 5 measured rounds one of the two responses carries an access token for a user id that does **not exist** in `users`. `userRepo.createUser` returns the object it was given, not the row `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` actually stored, and `getOrCreateWalletUser` trusts it.

## Recommendation

Make the wallet create path read back the stored row (or `RETURNING` it) and use THAT id, or fail and retry the lookup when the returned row's `wallet_address` does not match. Add a concurrency cell against a real Postgres (Seat J's native recipe). This is the same "fabricated object, not in the table" class KS-806 names; #1476 removes the collision between different wallets but not this race between two requests of the same wallet.

## Detail

* **Measured** (gate probe P4, real Postgres 15 built from the repo's init SQL + 49 migrations, app role `secuura_app` under RLS, the real route, real `/register`, real `userRepo`, real 039 lookup): 5 rounds of `Promise.all([login(A), login(A)])` for a fresh address A. Every round: both statuses 200, exactly 1 row. `idsInDb` per round: `[true,true]` (same id) once, then `[false,true]`, `[true,false]`, `[true,false]`, ... so in 4 of 5 rounds one returned id is not in the table. The token for that id then works until something looks the user up.
* **Where:** `services/auth/src/routes/wallet.ts` `getOrCreateWalletUser` (lookup, then `userRepo.createUser(user)` with a fresh `uuidv4()`), and `userRepo.createUser`'s upsert on `email_lookup_hash` returning its input.
* **Not caused by #1476:** the same shape exists on develop; with the old 8-character email the collision made it worse (every second wallet), with the new email it only happens for a true double submit of one address.
* Evidence: `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1476/logs/probe_head.out` (line 4) and `gateprobe1476.test.ts` (cell P4).

Provenance: Opus QA gate on #1476, verdict `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1476/verdict.md` (sha256/16 `b4615b4a35be26fb`), Minor-4; filed by Seat V 3rd on Wednesday's instruction. Related: KS-806, KS-1460 (`updateUser` callers that discard the result), KS-1052.

title: pre-push gate: pushing a branch that is not checked out skips the preflight, because the hook diffs HEAD and not the pushed commits
description:
**BLUF.** `.githooks/pre-push` decides whether to run the preflight from `HEAD` (`git diff --name-only "@{upstream}" HEAD` at `:80`, `"$_b" HEAD` at `:184`), and the preflight then tests the working tree. The refs git hands the hook on stdin are read only for the force-push check (`:48-69`). So `git push origin some-other-branch`, with a clean `HEAD` on another branch, skips the preflight for a `Blockchain/Dev` change in the branch actually pushed. The push lands with no `[pre-push]` output. Pre-existing; identical in the tip's hook, `302d8d081` and the KS-884 fix. Found by the KS-884 ref matrix (scenario S15).

**Recommendation.** Make the hook judge what is pushed, not what is checked out. Read the stdin lines (`<local ref> <local sha> <remote ref> <remote sha>`) and:

1. Compute the changed set per pushed ref from `<local sha>` against its base, not from `HEAD`.
2. Because the preflight tests the working tree (HEAD), also FAIL CLOSED: when a pushed `<local sha>` is not `HEAD` and it changes `Blockchain/Dev`, refuse with a clear message ("check out what you push, or push with the bypass deliberately"), rather than run the wrong tree. Running the preflight in a temporary worktree of the pushed sha is the heavier alternative.
3. Handle the shapes the stdin loop already skips: branch deletes (`<local sha>` all zeros), brand-new remote branches, tags (`refs/tags/...`), and multi-ref pushes (`--all`, several refspecs).
   Add a test cell per shape (red against today's hook for the unchecked-out branch). Not built here; this is the larger of the two KS-884 follow-ups because it changes what the hook refuses.

**Detail.**

* Measured 2026-10-12 by Seat F 17th. Scenario S15: `b-other` carries a `Blockchain/Dev` change, `HEAD` is back on a clean branch at `origin/develop`, then `git push origin b-other` to a local bare remote. Result SKIP for the tip's hook, `302d8d081`'s hook and the KS-884 fix; the saved push output is only git's two `To ...` / `* [new branch]` lines, so nothing tells the pusher the gate did not run.
* Why it is more than a corner case: `git push origin <name>` from a different checkout is an ordinary shape (a seat pushes a sibling branch, or a script pushes a ref), and the result reads like a green push.
* Evidence: `5_Project_History/2026-10-12_seatF-17th/ks884_ref_matrix.sh` (S15) and `ks884_matrix_full_OLD.txt`, `ks884_matrix_full_CURRENT_302d8d0.txt`, `ks884_matrix_full_FIXED.txt`.
* Related: KS-884 (PR #1474). Not caused or changed by it.

title: systemTest: the pre-rotation key is dead after rotate:true (split from KS-568 row 4) — waits on KS-577 revoke-on-rotate
description:
## Summary

[KS-568](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-568/systemtest-schemathesis-sk-connector-identity-regression-coverage-ks) row 4 proves that read-back survives key rotation. Kam ruled on 2026-08-07 that rotation must also **revoke the prior key**. As shipped, `rotate: true` mints a new key and leaves the old one valid with identical scopes. So a row-4 test that checks only the new key passes while the compromised credential stays live.

This ticket is the fourth assertion, **the old key is dead after rotation**. It's split from [KS-568](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-568/systemtest-schemathesis-sk-connector-identity-regression-coverage-ks) on 2026-10-06 so that [KS-568](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-568/systemtest-schemathesis-sk-connector-identity-regression-coverage-ks) can close on what holds today: rows 1–3, row 4's read-back half, rows 5–8 (row 5 is unblocked by [KS-578](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-578/cross-tenant-api-key-revoke-misses-the-db-row-when-the-cache-is-cold), Deployed to UAT), and the two-tier key provisioning.

## Waiting on

[KS-577](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-577/rotate-true-mints-a-new-key-but-never-revokes-the-old-one-implement) (Kamil, **In Review** as of 2026-10-06): implement revoke-on-rotate and agree the cutover window. The cutover window decides the assertion's timing: immediately dead, or dead after N seconds.

## Test

* Anchor under an operational key → `rotate: true` → the **old** key gets an auth error on read and on write, and the write creates no row (no 2xx-with-no-effect).
* Run with a warm and a cold key cache, the [KS-578](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-578/cross-tenant-api-key-revoke-misses-the-db-row-when-the-cache-is-cold) lesson.
* Red on `develop` today, green once [KS-577](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-577/rotate-true-mints-a-new-key-but-never-revokes-the-old-one-implement) merges. It could land early as `xfail(strict=True)` citing [KS-577](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-577/rotate-true-mints-a-new-key-but-never-revokes-the-old-one-implement), so it flips loudly. Peter's call once [KS-568](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-568/systemtest-schemathesis-sk-connector-identity-regression-coverage-ks) is in review.
* Appears on all three surfaces (console, Schemathesis results, HTML report).

## Also gated by [KS-577](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-577/rotate-true-mints-a-new-key-but-never-revokes-the-old-one-implement)

[KS-568](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-568/systemtest-schemathesis-sk-connector-identity-regression-coverage-ks)'s conditional bulk re-key extension waits on [KS-576](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-576/bulk-re-key-one-admin-authorised-rotate-across-a-named-set-of) (Todo, Kamil), which is blocked on [KS-577](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-577/rotate-true-mints-a-new-key-but-never-revokes-the-old-one-implement) by ruling. It stays out of [KS-568](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-568/systemtest-schemathesis-sk-connector-identity-regression-coverage-ks), and out of this ticket, until [KS-576](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-576/bulk-re-key-one-admin-authorised-rotate-across-a-named-set-of) exists in code.

Refs: [KS-568](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-568/systemtest-schemathesis-sk-connector-identity-regression-coverage-ks) (parent work) · [KS-577](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-577/rotate-true-mints-a-new-key-but-never-revokes-the-old-one-implement) (blocker) · [KS-578](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-578/cross-tenant-api-key-revoke-misses-the-db-row-when-the-cache-is-cold) · [KS-576](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-576/bulk-re-key-one-admin-authorised-rotate-across-a-named-set-of) · [KS-583](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-583/dr-rehearsal-lose-a-key-re-key-read-back-survives-on-pre-loss-anchors) (DR rehearsal step 4, same property) · [KS-492](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-492/review-g-systemtest-all-tools-security-regression-coverage) (Review G). title: systemTest: owner-scoped cross-tenant /api/status test (split from KS-588 test 5) — waits on KS-692's bind-creator half
description:

This is the genuine cross-tenant form of [KS-588](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-588/systemtest-schemathesis-apistatus-authorization-revoked-session)'s test 5, split out on 2026-10-06 so that [KS-588](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-588/systemtest-schemathesis-apistatus-authorization-revoked-session) can close on what's testable today (tests 0–4, 6–8, plus the interim posture).
